title: An AWS VP shares the 2 biggest AI mistakes he sees in job interviews
summary: AWS VP and distinguished engineer Marc Brooker said that it's "obvious" when someone hasn't kept up with AI developments.
content: Marc Brooker said he sees job seekers make two AI mistakes during interviews. AWS An AWS VP and distinguished engineer said he sees job seekers making two AI mistakes in interviews. The VP, Marc Brooker, said the first mistake is an under-reliance on AI. It's also an issue to over-rely on it, he said, because you offload your thinking. Job seekers want to show they're fluent in AI without suggesting they rely on it too heavily. Communicating that sweet spot can be tricky. Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, said he commonly sees both over- and under-reliance in interviews — and it can be a costly mistake. Brooker said it's increasingly clear when candidates haven't kept pace with how quickly the field has changed over the past year. "It's very obvious when people haven't tried the tools, been building hands-on, been using this new technology, and spending time deeply understanding how it works," Brooker said. He said it can be challenging, even as a leader, to keep up. It can also be difficult to differentiate between a trend and a meaningful update. Identifying that difference requires good taste and a lot of communication with others in the field, Booker said. Personally, he said he dedicates eight hours a week to intentional learning, some of which he does in parallel with building. At least some of this time is set aside for experimenting with new techniques, new tools, papers, and keeping up with the long-term durable trends. This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with AWS engineers and executives. To be alerted when the next piece publishes, follow reporter Ana Altchek here. AWS principal engineer says the best engineers are 'paranoid and lazy' when it comes to AI What defines an 'exceptional engineer,' according to the chief AI and technology officer at AWS AWS's Matt Wood has an AI agent help plan his outfit every day The other mistake Booker says he sees is over-relying on the tech. That involves a mindset of, "'I'm just going to ask AI to do this for me,'" or, "'I'm going to hand this question to my agent and answer it.'" Those applicants aren't thinking through answers and design questions. "I want to hire people who can think," Brooker said. "I want to hire people who can deeply consider trade-offs. I want to hire people who can communicate and understand and engage with the technology." Brooker said that simply typing in a problem and then asking an LLM or AI agent to solve it, "isn't a particularly useful or valuable skill." However, the VP said that it's "very useful and valuable" to know when to use AI and when to think for yourself. His comments reflect a growing number of tech leaders who have said that judgment and taste are becoming the most important skills in the field, and that AI is increasingly automating work, leaving engineers with more time for higher-level decision-making. title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed. Past weather incidents have disrupted it before.
summary: In some years, spectators have been injured by falling debris after strong winds sent parade balloons crashing into streetlights.
content: Bad weather has disrupted the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in the past. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in history. However, this isn't the first time that bad weather has disrupted the parade. After an incident during the 1997 parade, New York City set new limits on when the balloons could fly. This year's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been pushed to Saturday because of bad weather. It's the first postponement in the event's history, but storms and strong winds have caused trouble before. Over the years, rough conditions have grounded balloons, forced them to fly lower, and sent them crashing into spectators below. Here's a look at how bad weather has disrupted the parade over the years. 1971 Bad weather kept all the balloons on the ground during the 1971 parade. NBC via Getty Images In 1971, strong winds and heavy rain grounded all the parade's giant helium balloons for the only time in its history. The parade floats and performers still made their way down the street, The New York Times reported. 1993 A Sonic the Hedgehog balloon was punctured during the 1993 parade. This photo shows the character at a different year's parade. Charles Norfleet/Getty Images In 1993, strong winds pushed the then-new, 64-foot-tall Sonic the Hedgehog balloon into a streetlamp. The collision punctured the balloon and sent debris falling into the crowd below, injuring a man and a young girl, ABC7NY reported . 1997 The Cat in the Hat balloon struck a light pole during the 1997 parade. Evy Mages/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images In 1997, wind gusts of up to 43 mph damaged several balloons, including Barney and the Pink Panther, the Times reported. The Cat in the Hat balloon also hit a lamppost and snapped off its horizontal metal arm, which fell and struck several spectators below. Police told the Times that one of the victims suffered "very serious" injuries. Following the incidents in 1997, the city introduced new safety rules ahead of the 1998 parade. One barred large balloons from flying if sustained winds exceeded 23 mph or wind gusts exceeded 34 mph. 2005 An M&M balloon hit a lamppost during the 2005 parade, causing a light fixture to fall and injure several spectators. David Handschuh/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images In 2005, a balloon shaped like a giant M&M collided with a light pole, causing a light fixture to fall onto the crowd below. Two spectators, who are sisters, were left with cuts and bruises, the Times reported. 2019 The balloons flew lower than usual during the 2019 parade because of strong winds. Michael Loccisano/Getty Images In 2019, forecasts of strong winds prompted organizers to lower the balloons from their usual height of 55 feet to right above ground level for safety. title: The best, worst, and most unnecessary prequels in movie history
summary: "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is out now, after fans begged Suzanne Collins for Haymitch's story for years.
content: Haymitch and Effie return, albeit played by different actors, in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Lionsgate With a prequel, Hollywood can get as much out of intellectual property as possible. Prequels can also be a good way to illuminate something new about a story or character. Here are some of the best, worst, and plain unnecessary sequels in movie history. Before 2025, if you polled the average "Hunger Games" fan by asking whose games they wanted to see depicted on the page (or the screen), we'd be willing to bet that a majority would've said: Haymitch. Those fans got their wish this month, as " The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping " was finally released in theaters. It stars Joseph Zada as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy, the cranky mentor from District 12 first played by Woody Harrelson . The film (and the book it's based on) gave fans a new look at the horrors Haymitch had to endure both during and after the 50th Hunger Games. We won't spoil, but it's brutal. But for every "Sunrise on the Reaping," there's a "Mufasa," "Phantom Menace," or "Wonka" … and those aren't the only times Hollywood has released a prequel that may or may not be totally necessary. We've compiled a list of the 27 best, worst, or confusing prequels of all time — keep reading to see which films made the cut. There are two prequels in "The Hunger Games" franchise, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and "Sunrise on the Reaping." Joseph Zada in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Lionsgate The first "Hunger Games" prequel, " The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes ," was released in 2023. It's the story of the 10th Hunger Games, the first games that future president Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth) was involved in. It's also the story of the 10th victor, Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), who continues to haunt the narrative of Snow's life for 65 years. "Sunrise on Reaping" jumps ahead 40 years to the 50th Hunger Games, the games that Haymitch (Joseph Zada) wins. The story picks up with Haymitch's life in District 12, where he has a family, friends, and a girlfriend, Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak). After he's reaped, he meets many of our future faves, including Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning), Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), Wiress (Maya Hawke), and Mags (Lili Taylor). Both films add complexity and depth to the world of Panem, and they continue the social and political commentary themes that are so central to Katniss' story . Not only do we like these movies, but we'd take any more prequels Suzanne Collins wants to give us. In contrast to the coming "Hunt for Gollum," we were excited about "Furiosa," the prequel to "Mad Max: Fury Road." Anya Taylor-Joy in "Furiosa." Warner Bros. There have been four movies set in the world of " Mad Max ," a postapocalyptic future where the entire planet looks like a desert and society has almost completely broken down — and we can't get enough. The 2015 installment, "Mad Max: Fury Road," introduced audiences to Imperator Furiosa (played by Charlize Theron), a general who fights against the tyrannical Immortan Joe (played by Hugh Keays-Byrne) to free his enslaved wives. As "Fury Road" is technically a "Mad Max" movie, we spend more time with Max (played by Tom Hardy in "Fury Road" and originally played by Mel Gibson in the first three), but everyone left the theater wanting more Furiosa. While " Furiosa " may have underperformed at the box office, it was still so great to be back in the world created by director George Miller . Anya Taylor-Joy did a solid job as Furiosa, but it was Chris Hemsworth's performance as Dementus that we couldn't stop thinking about. Another amazing prequel? "The Godfather Part II." Robert De Niro in "The Godfather Part II." Paramount "The Godfather Part II," released in 1974, is both a sequel and a prequel to 1972's " The Godfather ." The film simultaneously follows Al Pacino's Michael Corleone as he assumes the role of don in the Corleone crime family after the death of his father Vito, and tells viewers the origin story of a young Vito (played by Robert De Niro) as he immigrates to New York City from Italy. Comparing and contrasting Vito and Michael at similar ages is a fascinating look into each of their personalities, and the film keeps viewers equally invested in both as they rise to power. The less we say about "The Godfather Part III," the better. "Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again" follows a similar format, and it's also a total banger. Universal Pictures In our opinion, " Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again ," released in 2018, is far superior to the 2008 original film. Why? Because it somehow follows "The Godfather Part II's" playbook and is both a sequel and a prequel. While we watch a grown-up Sophie (Amanda Seyfried) struggle to finally open her mother Donna's hotel in the present, we also get to look back at how a young Donna (played by the effervescent Lily James) met the three very handsome men, any one of whom could be Sophie's father. It shouldn't work, but it does. All we know is that — even if it doesn't make sense — we need both James and Meryl Streep back for the rumored third film. "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" is a perfectly entertaining film, whether you've seen the other two films in the trilogy or not. "The Good, the Bad and The Ugly"/Produzioni Europee Associati "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly," released in 1966, was the third and final film of director Sergio Leone's "Dollars Trilogy," which began with 1964's "A Fistful of Dollars." But "The Good..." is actually a prequel, as it depicts Clint Eastwood's character (known simply as The Man with No Name) gaining the iconic items of clothing he wears in the other two films, and it explicitly takes place during the Civil War, while the others seem a bit more modern. However, you don't need to see "Fistful" or its 1965 sequel to understand why "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" rules. It's a staple of the spaghetti Western genre, Eastwood is as good as he's ever been, and the film's theme is still iconic almost 60 years later. "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom" is a controversial film, but there are still things to enjoy about it. ‘Indiana Jones And The Temple Of Doom’/LucasFilm Yes, "Temple of Doom," released in 1984, takes place before 1981's "Raiders of the Lost Ark," even though characters from "Temple of Doom" (e.g. Ke Huy Quan's Short Round or Kate Capshaw's Willie Scott) are not mentioned in "Raiders" or "Last Crusade." Instead, "Temple of Doom" is a rip-roaring adventure following archaeologist/treasure hunter Indiana Jones (Harrison Ford) as he goes up against a religious sect that uses enslaved children and rips out human hearts while trying to save a rural village that's been cursed. "Temple of Doom" has not aged well in all aspects (its depiction of Indian food and culture is abysmal), and it doesn't really provide any context about Indy's early life — you'd have to watch the prologue of "Last Crusade" to see River Phoenix playing a younger version of the character — it's still worth the watch for the mine car chase, Ford's delivery of "We are going to die," and the ludicrous plane-crash scene. "Rogue One" is the best "Star Wars" prequel — bar none. Lucasfilm "Rogue One" is a prequel that explains exactly one plot point from the first "Star Wars" movie, originally released in 1977. Almost 40 years later, in 2016, fans finally got the answer to this question: How did the Rebels get access to the schematics of the Death Star? Now we know: The daughter of an Empire engineer, Jyn Erso (Felicity Jones), teamed up with a ragtag crew comprised of a spy named Cassian Andor (Diego Luna), a reprogrammed Imperial droid named K-2SO (Alan Tudyk), a blind believer in the Force and his best friend (Donnie Yen and Jiang Wen), and a former Imperial pilot who turned good (Riz Ahmed), to steal the plans from an Imperial base on a suicide mission. " Rogue One " is such an effective prequel because it almost immediately gets you invested in these characters, and you already know the stakes because of the original trilogy — the fate of the galaxy is at stake. If that wasn't enough prequel action for you, don't fret. The Disney+ series "Andor" is itself a prequel to "Rogue One." "Star Wars: Episode III – Revenge of the Sith" is also a solid prequel. Lucasfilm It all led to this: "Revenge of the Sith," released in 2005, finally showed "Star Wars" fans how exactly Jedi prodigy Anakin Skywalker (Hayden Christensen) turned into one of the most terrifying villains of all time , Darth Vader. The final confrontation between Anakin and his erstwhile mentor, Obi-Wan Kenobi (Ewan McGregor), has basically become a meme at this point , but when you rewatch the movie, it still hits. These two actors are both operating at the top of their game, and you really feel the heartbreak coming from both of them. This film almost makes the mediocre first two films in the prequel trilogy (more on them later) worth it. "Bumblebee" gave audiences the chance to learn more about everyone's favorite yellow Transformer. Paramount Pictures After the truly mind-boggling events of 2017's " Transformers: The Last Knight ," which introduced the Knights of the Round Table and Merlin to the mythology, it was time to take the franchise back to basics. And one year later, they did by releasing " Bumblebee ," which takes the story back to 1987 and focuses on 18-year-old Charlie (Hailee Steinfeld). Charlie, who has just lost her father, finds Bumblebee in a scrapyard and begins to bond with him. The stakes are a little lower, the lore is a lot more digestible, and Steinfeld is easily the best protagonist the franchise has ever seen. "Transformers: Rise of the Beasts" is pretty good too — "Transformers" might be the only franchise that's truly benefited from prequels. Paramount Pictures In 2023, "Rise of the Beasts" was released. It's a bigger story than "Bumblebee" but not as incoherent as "Last Knight" or "Dark Side of the Moon." It also has a way more compelling cast of characters, led by Anthony Ramos as Noah Diaz, Dominique Fishback as Elena Wallace, and Pete Davidson as Mirage. Again, this movie is a prequel to the original films, taking place mainly in 1994 and largely ignoring the events of both "Bumblebee" and the later films. It's a fun time at the movies for anyone who simply likes to turn off their brain and watch giant robots beat each other up. Because, against all odds, "Transformers One" makes this list too. "Transformers One" was released in September. Paramount Pictures In 2024, audiences were treated to yet another movie focusing on the Transformers; this time it was an animated prequel about the origins of Optimus Prime, voiced by Chris Hemsworth, his best-friend-turned-archnemesis Megatron, voiced by Brian Tyree Henry, and Bumblebee, voiced by Keegan-Michael Key. To put it plainly: This movie rocks. The voice casting is impeccable, the animation is beautiful, and the story is genuinely compelling. "X-Men: Days of Future Past" was a fun way to see younger versions of our favorite characters while keeping around some of the original X-Men. 20th Century Fox The "X-Men" franchise has one of the most complicated chronologies in movie history — and much of that is made even more confusing with the events of 2014's "Days of Future Past," which sees characters from the original "X-Men" film go back in time to link up with the characters introduced in 2011's "X-Men: First Class" to change the future and hopefully save all of mutant-kind. But even with that complicated setup, this movie is a lot of fun . Seeing Hugh Jackman's Wolverine interact with the younger version of his mentor Professor X (played by James McAvoy) and his arch-enemy Magneto (Michael Fassbender) is entertaining, and the happy ending they manage to pull off for almost everyone feels earned. The only prequel Pixar has ever produced is "Monsters University," which doesn't match the highs of "Monsters, Inc.," but is still a prequel worth watching. Disney/Pixar "Monsters University" was released in 2013 , 12 years after we last saw Sulley and Mike, our resident scarers (and later comedians). The ending of "Monsters, Inc." should never be touched — it's perfect — so when it was announced that another film in this universe was coming, fans were a bit nervous. But the filmmakers managed to avoid ruining the end of "Monsters, Inc." by instead showing us how best friends Mike (Billy Crystal) and Sulley (John Goodman) met while they were attending Monsters University. Fans get some genuine insight into how this world works, how Mike and Sulley were able to bond even though they're total opposites, and even how their beef with Randall (Steve Buscemi) started. And before you ask: No, " Lightyear " isn't a prequel. "Alien: Covenant" is more connected to the original "Alien" films than its predecessor, "Prometheus." Fox The world of " Alien " is a big one — that's why there have been seven movies and a TV show. While 2012's "Prometheus" takes place in the same universe as "Alien," its 2017 sequel "Alien: Covenant" directly ties into the events of the earlier films by essentially retelling the events of 1979's "Alien." But this time, it explains how the horrifying xenomorphs were actually created by the evil Weyland-Yutani Corporation and how learning to control these creatures has always been their plan. Also, we have to shout out Michael Fassbender , whose dual performance as Walter and David is the highlight of this movie. Creepy androids are an important part of the "Alien" franchise, and he knocked it out of the park. But not all prequels are great — some are completely unnecessary, like "Oz the Great and Powerful," an origin story for the Wizard from "The Wizard of Oz." Sony Pictures Imageworks/YouTube " The Wizard of Oz " remains one of the greatest films of all time, even though it was released 87 years ago. That's probably enough of a reason to leave this story alone, but instead, there have been many attempts to create a worthy sequel of the film — none of them have lived up to the original. Sadly, neither does 2013's prequel "Oz the Great and Powerful," starring James Franco as the titular Oz. Part of the fun of "The Wizard of Oz" is that you don't really know how the Wizard got to Oz, and that mystery adds to the fantastical vibes of the land of Oz. But if you watch "Oz," you'll learn all about Oscar's career as a scam artist, how he manipulated everyone around him, and how he inadvertently created the Wicked Witch of the East. It's not a horrible movie, but it kind of diminishes the magic of the original film, and for that, it's unnecessary. "Wonka" is actually kind of good, but it's more fun to leave Willy Wonka as a complete enigma. "Wonka." Warner Bros. Pictures The fun part of "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory" is that, for all intents and purposes, we know nothing about the chocolatier. He's just an agent of chaos who lives in a factory with the Oompa-Loompas. The version with Johnny Depp attempts to add some backstory, which is pushing it, but Depp's Wonka is eerie as anything, so we'll let it slide. Paul King's 2023 origin story, starring Timothée Chalamet as Wonka, is entertaining and beautifully made — he's the genius behind the "Paddington" films, after all — but do I feel better knowing that Wonka has a traumatic past and a dead mom? Eh. We can't knock Emma Stone's performance in "Cruella," but did we really need an origin story for the Dalmatian-hating Cruella de Vil? Emma Stone in "Cruella." Laurie Sparham/Disney We know that anti-heroes are all the rage, but did Disney really expect us to start siding with a woman who wanted to skin 101 Dalmatian puppies for a coat? This 2021 film gives Cruella de Vil, the villain of the 1961 animated film, a convoluted backstory in which she clashes with a legendary fashion designer known only as the Baroness (Emma Thompson). It is fun to watch Stone and Thompson face off, the fashion is to die for, and it's overall a solid movie ... but there's no reason for it to exist . We didn't need to know any more about Cruella — and we definitely don't need a sequel. Many people loathe the "Hobbit" trilogy — "Lord of the Rings" fans were content with the original three films. Warner Bros. Simply put: "The Hobbit" films (2012's "An Unexpected Journey," 2013's "The Desolation of Smaug," and 2014's "The Battle of the Five Armies") are slow. While the first three "Lord of the Rings" movies are based on a 1,200-page tome, "The Hobbit" films are based on a 300-page novel (that's downright cute in comparison). Maybe "The Hobbit," which starred Martin Freeman as Bilbo Baggins, would've worked as a single film, but there was no reason for the story to be stretched out across three films — especially when we know exactly how it ends thanks to Bilbo's appearances in "The Fellowship of the Ring" and "The Return of the King," as played by Ian Holm. We'll see if "The Hunt for Gollum" is a more worthy prequel — "The War of the Rohirrim" didn't ease our anxieties. "300: Rise of an Empire" took everything that was not great about "300" and doubled down. Warner Bros. "300," the 2006 historical epic, isn't exactly a work of cinematic art, but it is entertaining, spawned many a meme, and sparked much interest in ancient Sparta. However, "Rise of an Empire," released in 2014, is both a prequel and a sequel and also takes place during the events of "300." You could argue it bites off more than it can chew. Plus, in our opinion, Sullivan Stapleton does not hold the screen the same way Gerard Butler does. As The New York Times' Nicolas Rapold put it , "Rise of an Empire" "[lacks] the momentum and bombastic je ne sais quoi of '300.'" "The Thing" didn't live up to the '80s original. "The Thing." Universal Pictures The 1982 John Carpenter classic "The Thing" was negatively reviewed upon its release, but it has since been reappraised as one of the best sci-fi/horror films of all time. The special effects alone remain horrifying 44 years later. The 2011 prequel, also called "The Thing," leads viewers right up to the first moments of the 1982 film, which completely removes the stakes — you know that everyone in the film is toast. As many critics noted, the 2011 version also didn't really deviate from the source material. NME's Owen Nicholls wrote, "The real mess lies in the fact that from Plot Point One until Act III we're treading over all-too-familiar snow prints." Just watch the original. "Star Wars: Episode I — The Phantom Menace" and "Star Wars: Episode II — Attack of the Clones" are just boring. Lucasfilm Think back to 1999 — the first "Star Wars" movie in 16 years is about to be released. You can't wait to see how director George Lucas is going to show fans how the Jedi chosen one, Anakin Skywalker, became the space fascist known as Darth Vader. You sit down with popcorn to view "The Phantom Menace" ... and you watch a movie that's about track blockades, contains a scientific explanation for the Force, and portrays the future Darth Vader as a whiny kid. Three years later, in 2002, you sit down once again to see "Attack of the Clones." Maybe they've course-corrected — but no. Now you have a whiny teenage Anakin Skywalker, the Jedi acting even more incompetently than they did in "Phantom Menace," and a movie that's just as boring. There's not a Han Solo-level character to be found. Skipping to "Revenge of the Sith" is the best way to view "Star Wars," trust us. "The Scorpion King's" only redeeming quality is that it started Dwayne Johnson on his path to movie stardom. Universal Pictures/"The Scorpion King" "The Scorpion King" is just a bad movie. The CGI is bad, the Rock hasn't mastered his on-screen persona yet (read: he does not have a personality in this movie), and there's really no reason we needed to see the Scorpion King's origin story: There's a scene dedicated to his origin story in "The Mummy Returns," and that tells us everything we need to know. It's a testament to Johnson's charisma because if this had been anyone else's first leading role, their career would've been over. "Mufasa: The Lion King" does not justify its existence. Young Taka (voiced by Theo Somolu) and Mufasa (Braelyn Rankins) in Disney's "Mufasa: The Lion King." Disney Prequels like this are tricky to pull off — we know that Taka will turn into the villainous Scar, who will one day push his brother off a cliff to his death, an act that traumatized so many '90s and 2000s kids. So, it's hard to get invested in him as a cute cub when we know what his future holds. Similarly, it's hard to get invested in the action when we know that basically every character on screen will be fine. There are so many scenes where Mufasa almost falls off a cliff, which is supposed to be foreshadowing but also has no dramatic tension since we know he will be OK (for now). The animation is better than in 2019's " Lion King " remake. However, it's still somewhat in the uncanny valley zone, and it's always going to be easier to animate a cartoon lion to have expressions than a photorealistic one. If you're really in need of a "Lion King" sequel, check out "The Lion King II: Simba's Pride." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Bird-watching in 'GTA 6' has the seal of approval from America's top birders
summary: A birding expert found all 60 birds listed in GTA 6, and called the game's depiction of bird-watching the "most accurate version" ever in a game.
content: Whooping cranes appear in GTA 6’s fictional Florida, though birding expert Nicholas Lund says they’re more common in the game than in real life. : Jon G. Fuller/VWPics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Bird-watching is one of myriad activities players can take part in in "GTA 6." 60 different birds can be watched, and birder Nicholas Lund found them all soon after release. He said in the "Audubon" journal that "GTA 6's" bird-watching is the "most accurate" ever in a game. "Grand Theft Auto 6" players can steal cars, run drugs, and evade the police. One player had another priority: finding every bird. Birding expert Nicholas Lund tracked down all 60 species listed in the game's bird catalog, searching wetlands, beaches, forests, a farm, and a zoo across Rockstar Games' fictionalized Florida . His verdict? "GTA 6" offers what feels like "the most accurate version of modern birding ever put to screen," he wrote in "Audubon," the magazine of the National Audubon Society . Named for renowned 19th-century ornithologist John James Audubon, the society is the premier birding organization in the US and has a history spanning over 120 years. The game's wildlife has attracted attention from birders as well as GTA fans. Ahead of its release, a post in Reddit's r/birding community drew excited replies from players who planned to catalog birds between missions. "I think the crime sprees are going to have to wait," the original poster wrote. Another responded: "I have found my people. Hopefully there’s an achievement for finding them all." In "GTA 6", players can use binoculars to "study" birds and add them to a progress menu. Lund wrote in "Audubon" that he approached the search much as he would in real life, looking in different habitats. This led to finding gulls and pelicans near the water, wading birds in wetlands, and smaller birds farther north. He found 50 species during roughly eight hours of play after launch. The following morning, he completed the list by spotting an American Barn Owl on a water tank. Rockstar advertised 62 bird species before launch. Lund said the bird progress screen listed 60, with several others appearing elsewhere in the game. He noticed inaccuracies, including the appearance of endangered Whooping Cranes more often than they would in the real world. But he praised the familiar landscapes and the traffic, noise, and litter that accompanied the birdsong. The hunt is one of several ways players are spending time in the game's expansive world. Some players have chosen to do virtual home repairs or even doomscroll. Sony said players logged 683 million hours on PlayStation 5 in the game's first four days. After completing his list, Lund returned to a more familiar GTA pursuit: He drove his car off a cliff into the ocean. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Read the pitch decks of 19 startups looking to disrupt dating apps and social networking that have raised millions
summary: Social networking and dating startups used these pitch decks and memos to raise capital and ink deals.
content: iStock; Rebecca Zisser/BI New social, professional networking, and dating startups are coming onto the scene. VCs and angel investors are funding some of these promising startups. Here are the pitch decks 19 startups used while raising rounds or getting acquired. A new generation of consumer social startups is emerging. From platforms focused on getting people to meet IRL to dating apps taking on Tinder or Hinge, startups are disrupting the digital social scene. Founders of these startups are tackling problems like loneliness , dating app fatigue , and general dissatisfaction with the current social media incumbents. Some founders come from Big Tech backgrounds, like the Instagram-heavy team behind photo-sharing app Retro, or the ex-Google employees building the social-mapping app PamPam. Gen Z founders are also throwing their hats in the ring, like Isabella Epstein with her IRL-focused app Kndrd, and becoming content creators along the way. Investors are taking notice. Meet 22 VCs and investors eyeing new social startups Some venture capital funds — such as French firm Intuition VC or gaming-focused firm Patron — have made tackling loneliness and relationships part of their investment theses. But it's not just friendship and dating that are ripe for disruption. Startups like Khosla Ventures-backed Gigi , Yale student-founded Series , Boardy, and Goodword have raised capital for AI tools to help people network more effectively or maintain professional relationships . "When people think about loneliness, they think about friends and family," Goodword CEO Caroline Dell told Business Insider. "But we spend most of our waking hours at work as professionals." Other startups, like social network Spill, have opened investment rounds to users themselves via the Wefunder platform. Meet the founders of 11 startups competing with dating app giants like Tinder It's not yet clear how many of these investments will pan out. Some startups are pre-revenue, while others are experimenting with monetization models (such as freemium). title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return just gave Denny's a viral marketing moment
summary: Denny's embraced Jensen Huang's links to the diner chain by reinstalling the plaque for Nvidia's founding booth and revisiting Nvidia's origin story.
content: Jensen Huang donned a Denny's apron at Nvidia GTC in 2025. Emma Cosgrove/Business Insider Denny's used Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia to reshare its role in the company's origin story. The chain said it reinstalled a plaque at the booth where Nvidia's three founders first met. Huang, a former dishwasher at Denny's, has repeatedly called the diner brand his "alma mater." Denny's turned Jensen Huang 's return into a very public serving of nostalgia. In social media posts on Wednesday, the diner chain used the Nvidia CEO's comeback to remind the internet that Huang once washed dishes, bussed tables, and served customers at Denny's — before he and his cofounders discussed the idea for Nvidia over coffee at one of its San Jose locations in 1993. "Some things you just don't take off the menu," Denny's wrote. "Jensen Huang is one of them." The posts said Denny's had reinstalled a plaque marking the booth where Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem talked through the idea that became Nvidia after learning earlier this month that it had been taken down. "Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on," the chain added in the post, which racked up over 3.9 million views on X and garnered thousands of comments across Instagram and Facebook. Every story starts somewhere. We’re proud to be part of Jensen’s. pic.twitter.com/WpWJdLFmIs — Denny’s (@DennysDiner) November 25, 2026 The marketing move came two days after Nvidia reinstated Huang as CEO following his 11-day resignation. Huang stepped down after admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife and as the company launched an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia's board reversed course on Monday after saying it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was satisfied that Huang's return posed no national-security risk. Denny's nostalgia play got a mixed reception Denny's has embraced its link to Huang before, including with its limited-edition Nvidia Breakfast Bytes , which launched around Nvidia's 2025 GTC conference. But the post's timing on Wednesday drew a range of responses split between disbelief, jokes, and criticism. "Taking it down and putting it back up as soon as he gets rehired is crazy work," Diana Regan, an Oakland-based content creator and comedian, commented on Denny's post on Instagram. Some users said the post was a bold choice given the circumstances of Huang's resignation and reinstatement . "Why celebrate a guy who had multiple affairs, in which it had a direct effect on the global economy through the stock market and his ties to the AI bubble?" one commenter wrote in a reply that received more than 6,000 likes. Another summed up their mood more simply: "Genuinely cannot tell if this is a bit or not." Still, the chain's connection to Huang is not manufactured. Huang has repeatedly described Denny's as his first "alma mater," saying the job taught him that no task was too small to do well. "I was probably Denny's best dishwasher," Huang told the Stanford Graduate School of Business in April 2024. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I couldn't afford culinary school, so I got a $10-an-hour bakery job. It taught me skills I still value today.
summary: I dropped out of college to pursue baking but couldn't afford culinary school. I found a bakery job that changed my career.
content: The author worked at a bakery to learn. Courtesy of the author I dropped out of college because I wanted to pursue my passion for baking instead of a 9-to-5 job. I couldn't afford culinary school, so I created a portfolio and approached local bakeries for work. I landed a $10-an-hour job that led to new opportunities and taught me how to pursue my dreams. When I was in college for a traditional four-year degree, I became disillusioned about getting a job post-graduation. When I really thought about the 9-to-5 positions I would be pursuing after school, my stomach would drop. I started thinking about what I did for fun and what would bring me joy, and baking came to mind immediately. I had been baking my whole life , but by college, I was inviting friends over to share my weekly baked goods . For my sweet 16, I asked for a subscription to Bon Appétit magazine and had a pancake party with my best girlfriends, where I made all the pancakes and experimented with different flavors. My dad was well aware of my passion for baking, but I still knew that he would not be supportive of a switch to culinary school. The author started working at a bakery in a small town. Courtesy of the author So I made an extreme decision to chase my baking dreams and moved out of Miami — where the rent was skyrocketing — to a smaller town . I couldn't afford culinary school Since I couldn't afford culinary school without my dad's financial help, I decided to pursue work experience. I put together a photo album of my best desserts as a portfolio to show prospective employers and went to bakeries all over town. Many explained they were family-run, while one suggested I obtain my Florida Certified Food Manager certification to increase my odds. I agreed and found a local restaurant supply company that offered the state's required course, followed by the certification exam. It was a small investment for me at the time, and I do feel like it gave me an edge. After I received my official certificate from the state, I went into a nearby bakery that, quite frankly, intimidated me. But I had already done the same thing half a dozen times all over town, and gotten my feet wet with rejection. The owner of this particular bakery was impressed by my portfolio and asked if I could begin the next day. She even offered me $10 an hour to start, rather than as an unpaid intern, which I was willing to do at the time just to gain some professional experience. I started working at a bakery I eventually worked my way up to being in charge of the vegan and gluten-free baked goods. It was around 2010, so I felt really proud to be given something new in the baking world to learn about and perfect. I bought a used textbook from the Culinary Institute of America on gluten-free baking and discovered the cookbooks of Isa Chandra Moskowitz, my favorite vegan chef to this day. Without the money for school, I thought the work experience was just as valuable. It was; I eventually used my experience at the bakery to get a job in a restaurant and start a small catering company on my own. After closely observing the business of running a bakery, I decided I wanted to work toward opening my own. With a restaurant position, I was able to start saving money and investing it right back into my own dessert catering business. I proudly tried to get that catering business off the ground, going to local farmers' markets and filling personal orders. I did that for about two years until life happened and my career path changed several times. The experience taught me not to let obstacles get in the way After I had my son, I went through the same process of thinking about what I love to do. Having done that once before made the thought process less intimidating; I was starting over in my career for a second time. Since that one big decision to drop out of a four-year university and get a job at a small-town bakery, there hasn't been one career leap that's phased me. If there's an obstacle, such as the cost of schooling, I have always found a way. For instance, I applied for a scholarship for my 200-hour yoga training, so that I could teach my own classes while I went back and finished my four-year degree. As a yoga instructor and owner of a small cleaning business, I worked my way through those last two years of college and eventually became an English teacher. Without having made that one terrifying decision nearly two decades ago to pursue my dream — despite the financial challenges — I know I wouldn't have eventually gained all the work experience I did. title: Elon Musk and SpaceX pledge a share each to every active Trump account
summary: SpaceX joins a growing number of companies that have decided to invest in Trump Accounts.
content: Elon Musk and SpaceX are jumping into Trump Accounts. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images SpaceX says it will give one share of its stock to every active Trump Account. Elon Musk says he'll personally match the number of shares donated as part of a broader commitment. SpaceX's COO has separately pledged more than 2 million of the rocket maker's shares. SpaceX said Wednesday that it will give one share of its stock to every active Trump Account . CEO Elon Musk will personally match the number of shares donated by the AI and rocket company, as "part of his pledge to donate one SpaceX share to every kid in America ," the company said. Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and chief operating officer, has also pledged more than 2 million SpaceX shares. "SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company behind Starlink, Starship, Grok, and X said in a press release. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit." Musk — the world's wealthiest person with an estimated $820 billion net worth, per the Bloomberg Billionaires Index — confirmed his commitment in a pinned post on X. "Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," he wrote. Musk said the share from SpaceX "will be transferred next month," while the share from him "will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year." The share from SpaceX will be transferred next month. The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026 A SpaceX share was worth about $127 as of Wednesday's market close, down 44% from its peak price of around $226 in mid-June, shortly after the company went public. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children born between 2025 and 2028. They were launched in July in an effort to broaden participation in the stock market and help families build long-term financial security. The US Treasury has been seeding each account opened with a one-time, $1,000 contribution. The White House said in early October that 70 million Trump Accounts had been created. It's unclear how many are considered "active," but if Musk and SpaceX were to transfer 70 million shares each, those gifts would be worth $8.9 billion separately or nearly $18 billion combined, based on Wednesday's closing price. SpaceX joins a growing number of companies that have decided to invest in Trump Accounts. Dell, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Charles Schwab, and BlackRock have also pledged contributions to the accounts. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Elon Musk floats a truly wild figure for SpaceX's potential value: $128 quintillion
summary: Elon Musk says SpaceX's value could jump 75 million-fold if it can colonize other planets and harness a tiny fraction of the Sun's energy.
content: Elon Musk says SpaceX could be worth an astonishing sum in the future. Jae C. Hong/AP Elon Musk says SpaceX could be worth around $128 quintillion, or 75 million times its value today. It would have to colonize other planets and harness a tiny fraction of the Sun's energy, he said. "I recommend holding on to your shares," Musk posted on X. Elon Musk is going galactic with his latest claim of what SpaceX might be worth one day: $128 quintillion. That's 128 billion billions, or 128 trillion millions, or 128 followed by 18 zeros: 128,000,000,000,000,000,000. "If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun's energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy," Musk said in an early morning X post on Thursday. The IMF puts the value of the world economy at around $128 trillion. Musk's post suggests SpaceX could be worth a million times that much, or $128 quintillion. That would be a roughly 75 million-fold increase from its $1.7 trillion market capitalization as of Wednesday's close. "These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them," Musk wrote. "I recommend holding on to your shares." If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun’s energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy. These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them. I recommend holding on to your shares. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026 Musk's post implies that a single SpaceX share, worth around $127 at Wednesday's close, could one day be worth $9.5 billion or so, assuming no dilution. The world's wealthiest man is no stranger to making wild, unfounded claims about SpaceX's potential value. He posted in October that the maker of Starlink, Starship, Grok, and X could eventually be worth " orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy." Musk later posted that wasn't a "statement of extreme confidence," but a belief that "there is such a path and the probability of achieving it is not zero." SpaceX generated $14.6 billion of revenue last quarter , up 161% from the same period last year, and swung from a $1.1 billion net loss to a $4.4 billion net income. Musk posted in October that SpaceX hitting $1 trillion in annual revenue in 2028 was " no longer impossible ." Even if it reaches that mark, then grows revenue another 1,000-fold to $1 quadrillion, that would still be less than 1% of $128 quintillion. He made his latest claim about SpaceX's potential price tag after pledging to match the company's gift of one share to every active Trump Account. The rocket maker said it was part of his commitment to give one of his SpaceX shares to " every kid in America " next year. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I quit my corporate job to open a cinnamon roll bakery. A year later, here's what surprised me most.
summary: Arin Senior left corporate finance to open a cinnamon roll bakery in NYC. A year later, she is working 100-hour weeks and but feeling more satisfied.
content: Arin Senior, a financial analyst, left her corporate finance job to open Spirals, a cinnamon-roll bakery in NYC. Eli Nathan/Spirals Arin Senior left her corporate finance job to open a cinnamon-roll bakery in NYC. Senior has never worked in a bakery before and found her scope of work to be surprising. Senior now works 100-hour weeks but would not trade it for her 9-to-5 corporate job. Arin Senior, 26, is the founder of Spirals, a cinnamon-roll bakery in New York City's East Village. She opened the shop in August 2025 after leaving her job as a strategic finance analyst at The Estée Lauder Companies. A Wharton graduate, Senior spent nearly two years developing the idea for Spirals before taking the plunge. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I spent years working in strategy and finance in the corporate beauty industry, but I always knew I wanted to open my own business and be my own boss. Last year, I finally took the leap. I opened Spirals, a cinnamon-bun bakery in New York City , after spending months developing recipes, finding a location, and figuring out everything that goes into starting a business. The day I signed the lease, I quit my corporate job and went all in. We opened in August 2025, and by October, we were profitable. A year into running the bakery, I've learned that being your own boss isn't necessarily about working fewer hours. It's about having more control over what you work on and how you spend your time. My corporate job felt monotonous Spirals, located in New York City's East Village, specializes in cinnamon rolls. Eli Nathan/Spirals My corporate job wasn't bad, but my role was monotonous. I knew exactly what every day would look like. When I was growing up, my dad had his own company, and I loved the lifestyle it gave him. I liked the idea of setting my own schedule and dipping my toe into a whole bunch of different things. I also noticed a gap in New York City's bakery scene . You could find cookies in every flavor, doughnuts, and croissants, but I couldn't find a really great cinnamon roll. I felt there was an opportunity. While still working in finance, I started developing flavors and recipes, researching how to set up an LLC, and looking for a storefront. My husband helped with the search for a space. We looked for about six months before finding the right one. I wanted to be involved in every part of the business. Instead of just evaluating the cost of one product, I could decide what products to launch, how to launch them, and who to market them to. The learning curve was steep Arin Senior has never worked in a bakery before opening Spirals. Eli Nathan/Spirals I'd never run a bakery before. In fact, I'd never even worked in one. The learning curve was steep. There wasn't necessarily one moment when I thought I couldn't do it. There were just a million things to figure out. One of the hardest parts was learning how to delegate. A lot of the strategic decisions start with me. I might decide what we want our menu to look like in June of next year, while my chef takes those ideas and figures out how to execute them. I also handle pricing, marketing, and the broader direction of the business. The biggest lesson I've learned about building a team is that attitude matters more than experience. Hiring and retaining good staff has been by far the hardest part of running the bakery. You can teach people a lot of things, but you can't teach a good attitude. Once I realized that, things got easier. I also had to learn social media from scratch. I'd never posted publicly or edited a video before starting Spirals. I experimented with what people liked, and learned by doing. TikTok initially brought in almost all of our business, alongside influencers who tried our products and posted about them organically. I'm working more hours now Arin Senior said she often works 100 hours a week now as a bakery owner. Eli Nathan/Spirals I think there's a misconception that becoming your own boss means working less. For me, it's actually been the opposite. I'm working 100-hour weeks pretty frequently. There are so many responsibilities I never thought about. The refrigerator breaks, the AC stops working, and suddenly I'm spending time figuring out maintenance issues. But I do have more autonomy over when I work. I can decide to work all day Sunday and take Monday off, or spread a few hours of work across the week. I can fit in a workout class in the middle of the day or travel to see someone on a weekday — things I couldn't have done in my corporate job. I also have a much greater sense of ownership. Almost everything happening at Spirals is something I've had a hand in building. That doesn't mean I never miss aspects of corporate life . I'm occasionally jealous of my husband, who can close his laptop on Friday night and not think about work until Monday. When something goes wrong at a big company, there's usually someone else to turn to. I don't think everyone needs to turn a passionate side project into a storefront in New York City. But having something you love outside your job can still make all the difference. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Mozilla Firefox head says the company is ‘ramping up' the time it devotes to cybersecurity issues
summary: "What we've seen is that we are devoting a lot more of our own resources in order to fix these things," Mozilla's Ajit Varma told Business Insider.
content: Firefox head Ajit Varma said there is still enough time to stay ahead of the AI cybersecurity wave. Alex Broadway/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images Mozilla's Firefox head says his team has stepped up its efforts to fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Ajit Varma said his team is working with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Varma said he still thinks there's "enough time" to fix bugs before the next AI advancements roll out. Mozilla's Firefox chief says the pace of AI advancements is still giving his team "enough time" to make sure it addresses any cybersecurity vulnerabilities. "What we've seen is that we are devoting a lot more of our own resources in order to fix these things," Mozilla's Ajit Varma told Business Insider during a recent interview. "So I think if you look at a year ago, I think it was about 10% of our time, and now, when I look at the latest, it's 27% of our effort is now spent on addressing these." Varma's comments came as top US government officials cautioned that the recent string of outages affecting everything from Microsoft Outlook to JPMorgan Chase reflects companies' efforts to fix software issues faster than ever. Home Depot's chief information officer recently told Business Insider that the retailer wants to cut the time it takes to deploy a fix "to hours." Varma said both OpenAI and Anthropic are giving Mozilla, which is a nonprofit, "a lot of tokens for free." The Firefox head said the frontier models "are finding more and more complicated vulnerabilities within our browser." The AI leaders are eager to work with Mozilla. So much so that Varma said that in March his team noticed that someone with an Anthropic email address had submitted a bug. Since Firefox is completely open source, anyone could do so. Once Mozilla's team got in touch, they realized that the Anthropic employee had found a lot more vulnerabilities. "They were excited about testing their models with Firefox, because we have spent decades building a very secure and very tested browser that's open source, has a lot of contributions and a lot of scrutiny around it," Varma said. Beyond cybersecurity, Varma said, is finding other ways to deploy AI tools to make "Firefox even faster" and prevent issues like memory leaks. He said he encourages his team to view AI as a tool and to "triage" what truly needs human attention. "We are trying to encourage people to say there's a lot of routine activities that we don't necessarily need humans to do and that AI does really well because it's relentless; it doesn't get tired," he said. title: I brought my family to New York for the Thanksgiving Day Parade. It's been on my bucket list since I was a kid, but now I won’t get to see it.
summary: Erin Finney traveled from Florida to NYC with her family to see Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. She can't stay for its Saturday rescheduling.
content: Erin Finney traveled to New York City with her family to see the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, but they will miss its rescheduled Saturday date. Provided by Erin Finney. Erin Finney had always dreamed of seeing the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade live. This year, she brought her family from Florida to New York to check it off her bucket list. They spent about $5,200 on flights and a hotel, but will miss the postponed parade. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Erin Finney, 43, who traveled with her family from Lakeland, Florida, to New York City to catch the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. It has been edited for length and clarity. The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been on my bucket list ever since I was a little girl. I remember going to my grandma’s house, sitting on the floor, and watching it on TV. Even after I got married and had kids, watching the parade was still my tradition. If we went camping for Thanksgiving, I'd still make sure I could catch it. We don't really have a big family back home anymore, and Thanksgiving hasn't felt quite the same. So, this year, I thought we should start doing destination Thanksgivings instead, and check off bucket-list No. 1: seeing the parade in person . I had it all mapped out I traveled to New York with my husband, our three teenage boys, and one of my son's girlfriends. We don't do a whole lot of family vacations with school and work, so this was the first proper one in a while. The boys had been to New York before, but only in the summer. This time, they were going to experience the city in the cold, with all the Christmas decorations up. It was her teenage sons' first time in New York City during the holiday season. Provided by Erin Finney. I spent months planning this trip. There were lots of schedules to rearrange, and I joined a Facebook group to pick up tips and tricks from people who had been to the parade before. We're from Florida, so we don't have a ton of cold-weather stuff. On top of shopping for clothes and making sure everybody had everything they needed, I spent more hours than I'd like to admit mapping out our week, what to do, and where to go. We're staying at a hotel near 48th Street and Sixth Avenue, within walking distance of the parade route. I knew where I was going to sit and had my alarm set for 3:30 a.m. so we could get out there early. I'd read that you couldn't bring chairs, so I bought shower curtains from Dollar Tree for us to sit on. I ordered rain shoes, too, just in case. We spent about $1,500 on flights and about $3,700 on our hotel. As part of the trip, Finney and her husband surprised their sons with tickets to a Giants game. Provided by Erin Finney. We got here on Sunday and went straight to New Jersey to catch a Giants game. It was a surprise for our boys since they play football. We were worried it would get rained out, but it didn't, so I thought the parade would be fine, too. Then came the unexpected news On Wednesday, I was in Brooklyn with my youngest to visit a comic-book store when my oldest son called. I freaked out, thinking somebody was hurt or something was wrong. When he told me the parade had been postponed due to bad weather , I thought he was joking. But then I looked it up, and my stomach dropped. Finney first heard the parade had been postponed through her son and initially thought he was joking. Provided by Erin Finney. I told my family to give me a minute to process what had happened. When I got to the subway, I sat down at the station and started crying. I kept thinking, "Why am I crying?" But I think it was all the excitement leading up to it, and how disappointed I was that I wouldn't get to see the parade after all. We were only meant to be in New York until Friday morning, so we won't be there for the rescheduled parade on Saturday. I looked into changing our flights, but it would have cost at least another $800, plus extra nights at the hotel and food for all of us. I'm also a nurse and am scheduled to work Saturday night, so staying would have meant calling in to work. It just wasn't feasible to extend the trip. The trip was planned around the parade, and Finney was disappointed when it was postponed. Provided by Erin Finney. The parade was the plan, so now we're trying to figure out what to do on Thanksgiving. We hadn't made plans for dinner, but now I'm hoping people might leave early and open up a table somewhere. I understand why the parade was postponed. Safety has to come first, and as a nurse, I would never want anyone to get hurt. I'm disappointed, but the trip has still been great. At the end of the day, it's Thanksgiving, and I'm with my family. I'm thankful for them. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: A teenage entrepreneur skipped the advice 'follow your passion.' His company did 6 figures in revenue in a month.
summary: Stavya Nilawar's agency brought in $119,000 in a month. The 19-year-old explains why he doesn't believe in the age-old advice to "follow-your-passion."
content: Stavya Nilawar founded his creator-marketing agency, Nilawar, with about $35. Courtesy of Stavya Nilawar Stavya Nilawar, 19, built a creator marketing agency that generated $119,000 in October 2026. He chose AI clients for their growing budgets, not because he loved the industry. His advice: Pick a business model you enjoy, then find a niche with demand. When seeking career advice, there's a refrain that comes up often: "Follow your passion." Stavya Nilawar, 19, thinks that approach can be a "huge limiter" for aspiring entrepreneurs. Rather than building a business around a personal passion, Nilawar selected an industry where he saw demand, companies with marketing budgets, and room for a service provider like him. His creator-marketing agency, Nilawar , connects brands with content creators for sponsored segments and dedicated videos. The agency, which he launched with about $35, works with AI companies including CodeRabbit and Wispr Flow, and typically earns a cut of each project fee. The business brought in $119,000 in revenue in October 2026 , according to business-account statements reviewed by Business Insider. Nilawar's first attempt at entrepreneurship was much more closely tied to his interest in social media. He started a social-media marketing agency, visiting local businesses to film and edit short-form videos for their accounts. He'd create about 30 videos a month for clients and earn roughly $750 for his work. "Quickly, I realized doing that all myself — the editing, the recording, and going to the actual place — it was so much time," Nilawar, a sophomore at Babson College, said. "That time cost was insane." He knew he wanted to work in media, but he didn't necessarily want to be the person on camera or have a business dependent on his physical presence. "I didn't want to be the main figure," he said. "But I knew that I could work with other people who can be the main figure." So when he launched Nilawar, he chose a model that suited him: running an agency that connects brands with creators. The next decision was which kinds of brands to serve. He picked AI for the business opportunity, not personal interest Nilawar decided to focus on AI. He saw that AI companies were growing quickly and often had budgets for creator partnerships — the type of work his agency could facilitate. "I was not passionate about AI at all, to be honest," he said. He believes founders should look beyond whether an industry sounds exciting or aligns with their personal interests and, instead, seek niches with customers who have both a clear need and the ability to pay. For him, that meant working with AI companies instead of focusing on an industry he was personally passionate about. "The business vehicle you choose should be something you like," he said. "But then after that, the niche you do should always be business-oriented." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Wall Street wants to understand Gen Z. These high schoolers are giving it a crash course.
summary: High school founders Jasper Gould and Emile Chilingirian have turned their expertise on Gen Z and finance into a 28,000-subscriber newsletter.
content: High school students Emile Chilingirian and Jasper Gould cofounded a finance newsletter. Jasper Gould Jasper Gould cofounded Passing the Torch, a finance and economics newsletter with 28,000 subscribers. The newsletter offers something many others don't: An authentic Gen Z perspective. The newsletter has attracted Wall Street bros as well as young folks interested in finance. Finance analysts sift through heaps of consumer data, conduct large-scale surveys, and meticulously track trends in their quest to understand Gen Z. High school senior Jasper Gould had a better idea. Gould and Emile Chilingirian of New York City cofounded Passing the Torch , a finance and economics newsletter that's amassed 28,000 readers since its official launch in 2025. The newsletter offers an unfiltered glimpse into the minds of Gen Z , the latest generation to drum up spending power. Passing the Torch reports on a wide breadth of topics, from how Zoomers perceive automated vehicles and robotaxis to a deep dive into Pershing Square Capital Management's $65 billion now-defunct takeover bid for Universal Music Group . This month, the duo published an article titled "AI Stocks Just Started Taking Accutane," which discusses the recent tech stock sell-off. Subscribers pay $15 a month, or $150 annually. "We are a proprietary data source of a very special order, and I think people recognize that," Gould, 18, told Business Insider. That's one reason the newsletter has garnered a fan base on Wall Street. "When we looked into the subscriber logs, we saw a concentration at firms like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Chase, and Blackstone," Gould said. 'Let's make a business' Although Gould and Chilingirian are now in the media business, they got their start in the nonprofit sector. They cofounded Brooklyn Youth Charitable Investment Group, an organization that teaches financial and leadership skills to high schoolers, in 2024. The nonprofit has 100 active members and over 1,000 students have participated so far. To gain investors, the pair did cold reach-outs while juggling school and their personal lives. "There was a period of time in 10th grade where we were getting three hours of sleep a night, and I'm very happy we were doing so," Gould said. "If you are intentional about your relationships, if you really invest in them, and if you have something going for you like being in high school, that's really all it takes to warm things up." That helped them secure guest speakers from major institutions like Deutsche Bank, the White House, and Apple, Gould said. As the nonprofit grew, Gould and Chilingirian decided to create an Instagram account to share more tips and advice for young folks interested in finance. The account gained over 37,000 followers in less than two years, which inspired Gould and Chilingirian to think bigger. "A lot of the things we're saying are really valuable to investors, so let's make a business," Gould said. They said they didn't have to purchase ads or flood X to find readers. "It was word of mouth, stakeholders in the nonprofit, and people who knew us," Gould said. "In our pursuit of fundraising and working on this organization, we sent a lot of emails, and we had a lot of people in our network." On-the-ground journalism There are certainly challenges to running a media business, including competing in an oversaturated media market and making money amid dwindling online ad rates. There's also the fact that they're still in high school. "The biggest issue is getting people to take us seriously, which generally isn't an issue after the first phone call, but it's always a battle leading into it," Gould said. While the pair conduct traditional research and speak with experts, their youth allows them to take an anthropological approach to tracking Gen Z's tastes. "Just go to a party and ask someone," Gould said. "They don't realize that what they're about to tell us is going to end up making some investor or some company millions of dollars." Although neither founder has graduated from high school yet, they've already envisioned how their brand will continue leveling up. These days, that includes offering their deep insights into Gen Z to companies through consulting. "I'm sure there are some analysts at some of the pod shops that are learning how to read TikTok and Reddit as valuable sources of information, but I'm seeing it in the hallways every day," he said. title: Bye bye, gift cards: People are putting more effort into gifts this year
summary: National Retail Federation data shows holiday shoppers cutting gift card purchases, favoring personal, budget-conscious gifts instead.
content: The number of people planning to give gift cards this holiday season is at a 20-year low. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images People are planning to buy fewer gift cards as holiday gifts this year. Gift card purchases are expected to hit a 20-year low, according to the National Retail Federation. It shows that shoppers are getting more thoughtful about their gift-giving. Expect to get fewer gift cards this holiday season. The share of consumers who are planning to buy someone on their list a gift card is at the lowest in more than two decades, according to a survey of likely Thanksgiving Weekend shoppers conducted by the National Retail Federation, or NRF. Just 39% of shoppers surveyed plan to buy a gift card this year. Two decades ago, a majority did. The gift card 's slide in popularity can be attributed to factors from generational divides to giving fewer gifts, retail experts said. But it also shows a societal shift: If shoppers are going to bother buying a gift, it might as well mean something. "While gift cards are flexible, they are neither imaginative nor are they particularly personal," Global Data retail analyst Neil Saunders said. "A lot of people now want to give more meaningful gifts." The NRF found something similar in its survey, said Allison Zeller, the group's vice president of industry and consumer insights. The top reason respondents said they weren't giving gift cards was that they wanted to give gifts more tailored to the recipient. There was also an age divide, with baby boomers reporting they were more likely to give a gift card than Gen Z shoppers were, Zeller said. Thanks to the internet — and now AI tools — shoppers also have fewer excuses for not finding a good gift. That's a shift from two decades ago, when more shoppers stuck to in-store shopping during the holiday season. "You were limited in what you could buy based on what was in your town," she said. This year, many consumers are also trying to save money on holiday gifts. One-fifth of respondents to the NRF's survey, for instance, said that they were planning to buy gifts for fewer people . That could point to another reason people are buying fewer gift cards, said Julian Givi, an associate professor of marketing at West Virginia University who has studied gift-giving and consumer behavior. For years, gift cards were an easy choice if buyers didn't know the recipient that well — think about that cousin you only see twice a year, Givi said. "If you cut them out, you're probably cutting out the gift card spending," he told Business Insider. Shoppers who are trying to save money on holiday gifts are also more likely to buy a gift at a big discount during shopping days like Cyber Monday, Givi said. Those kinds of deals can give the gift recipient the impression that the giver spent more than they actually did, he added. Gift cards, meanwhile, make the purchase price obvious. "You don't want to make it so apparent to people what you're spending whenever times are kind of tough," he said. Do you have a story idea to share?
