title: I moved back to Scotland after 19 years in the US. Thanksgiving is the one tradition I refuse to give up.
summary: After 19 years in the US, I brought Thanksgiving home to Scotland. Celebrating it abroad has become an important family tradition.
content: The author moved back to Scotland in 2020 but still celebrates Thanksgiving. Courtesy of the author I moved to the US in 2001 knowing nothing about Thanksgiving, but it quickly became a holiday I loved. Since moving back to Scotland in 2020, I've kept celebrating Thanksgiving despite a few challenges. Celebrating Thanksgiving in Scotland feels strange, but it keeps me connected to my life in the US. When I moved to the US to study abroad in 2001, I was baffled by the traditions of Thanksgiving. As the years went by, however, I developed a real appreciation for this American holiday — even if I've never quite been able to wrap my head around adding marshmallows to sweet potato. In my early years in the US, I attended Thanksgiving dinners because everyone around me did. Over time, though, I grew to love the simplicity of the holiday — so much so that I brought the tradition home with me when I returned to the UK after 19 years. It's a holiday about gratitude, not gifts I love that there's no pressure around buying gifts or religious ceremony — Thanksgiving is about spending time with people I love, being community-minded, and giving thanks for the small things in life. In Colorado, I'd host friends who didn't have family nearby Courtesy of the author When I lived in the US, I ran in the local Turkey Trot to raise money for charity every Thanksgiving morning, and taught a special gratitude-themed yoga class afterwards. I hosted dinners for friends who also didn't have family nearby and learned to make my own cranberry sauce, adding some dishes from Scotland, like my mom's leeks in cheese sauce. My homemade pumpkin cheesecake became an annual request. When I moved back to Scotland after nearly two decades in the US, I didn't expect that an American holiday would become one of the things that helped me feel at home again . It helped me with a major life transition My first year back in Scotland was a whirlwind of finding a job, a new home, and establishing new routines. Once things settled down, though, I realized how much I missed having an annual occasion to celebrate the good things in life. While my friends in the US were readying their turkey dinners or making plans to fly home and be with family, here in Scotland, life just carried on as normal. The days were getting shorter and colder, and I was in desperate need of some festive cheer to warm my spirits. It was my partner who suggested we celebrate Thanksgiving. Courtesy of the author It was my English partner who suggested we host our own Thanksgiving meal in Scotland. He had a friend from the US who was always homesick at this time of year, and we thought his two kids would relish the opportunity to experience an American holiday that they've only seen in movies. It's strange celebrating a holiday when the rest of the country goes to work My partner volunteered to take on the turkey, and I made a shopping list for the rest. Getting the basics was pretty easy, but some items weren't so readily available. After a half day of searching, I finally found canned pumpkin at a local health food store (at nearly $5 a can), and my American friend saved the day with a bag of fresh cranberries. Our teenager even took a break from his Rubik's Cube to peel sprouts, but it didn't last long Courtesy of the author It felt a bit strange celebrating a holiday when the rest of the country was at work. The kids went to school, I had to prep the meal between work tasks, and there would be no day off on Friday to recover. After school, the day took on an atmosphere of excitement, however. The kids enjoyed the novelty of a holiday their school friends weren't celebrating, and my stepson even put down his Rubik's Cube for 20 minutes to help prepare the sprouts. A few friends crowded into our kitchen, and we managed to find the football game on satellite television, although I don't think anyone understood the rules. Our first Thanksgiving was quite traditional, with all the classics Courtesy of the author Once dinner was ready, taking turns to say what we were grateful for felt unfamiliar to some of my guests, but everyone joined in. The funniest part was seeing my friends' faces when our American friend presented his sweet potatoes with marshmallows. At times, everyone looked as bewildered as I felt on my first Thanksgiving, but it turned out to be a tradition that can easily translate across cultures. For most other people in Scotland, it was just an average Thursday night, but for the first time in a year, I felt really connected to the life I'd left behind. Living abroad taught me that home isn't just where you come from Since 2021, we've found a way to honor Thanksgiving almost every year. Sometimes it's just a quiet dinner with my partner and his daughter; last year, it coincided with a visit from our Swedish friends, and we ended up with a large group crammed into my tiny apartment . Last year it coincided with a visit from our Swedish friends, so we all crammed into my tiny apartment Courtesy of the author I've found that people from all over the world are really interested in the ideas behind Thanksgiving, and are usually thrilled to be invited over. I can't believe that a can of pumpkin puree here costs more than a gallon of gas in the US, and I still haven't found a reliable source of fresh cranberries. But I've learned handy substitutes, like using butternut squash or sweet potato puree for pumpkin, and red currants or sour cherries for cranberries. Scotland may be where I grew up, but moving back after 19 years wasn't quite as simple as I expected. I left friends, routines, and the life I'd built behind. Keeping Thanksgiving alive has helped me hold on to that part of myself while making a new life here. Next year, I want to organize my own mini Turkey Trot before dinner — even if we all have to get up early and fit it in before work. It's one more American tradition I can make my own, wherever home happens to be. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I’m a Silicon Valley couples therapist. Here’s what Jensen Huang's daily therapy sessions might entail.
summary: Here's what Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's daily therapy sessions might include, according to a Silicon Valley therapist who treats high-profile couples.
content: Phil Boissierie has been a couples' therapist in Silicon Valley for almost 20 years. Courtesy of Phil Boissierie At an Nvidia all-hands, reinstated CEO Jensen Huang said he'll be in therapy for 90 minutes a day. Phil Boissierie is a Silicon Valley therapist who works with couples in high-profile careers. He hasn't met Huang but says therapy could include managing public pressure and relationship repair. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Phil Boissierie, a 50-year-old marriage and couples therapist at The Relationship Therapy Group in Silicon Valley. His words have been edited for length and clarity. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently said he was doing 90 minutes of therapy every day as part of his effort to move forward. I've been a couples therapist in Silicon Valley for 20 years. Ninety minutes of therapy a day is not particularly common, nor is it a traditional model. Usually, if someone's doing that much therapy every day, it's because they're likely trying to work through a lot quickly and create some behavioral change. If a behavior is compulsive or hard to change, doing extended periods of therapy every day can be helpful for building traction. I can't say for sure what he's doing since I don't know Jensen, but here's what that frequency of therapy for a high-profile CEO in a situation like this would probably look like. There will be a lot to work through Working through how to manage public pressure, understand repetitive behavior, and repair relationships are all things I would discuss in the first few sessions of intensive therapy like this. The pressure, the eyes on him , the eyes on the company — all of that is huge, alongside all the damage that's been created in his relationships with his wife, his family, and the other people he's been involved with and working with. Do you think Jensen Huang should have been reinstated? Take our survey . Any therapy plan has to do with what the particular person is going through, and I'm not going to speculate, but in my practice, a lot of times when we see someone having multiple affairs , that doesn't just come out of nowhere. It often has to do with family of origin, early life experiences, and things they're working through, which become the fabric of who we are and how we operate. It takes intentional work to create those changes. I also always recommend to people that when a disclosure comes out about an affair, doing work as a couple right up front is really important. If Jensen and Lori Huang are also doing couples work, I think that would be really, really smart and not overkill. The 90-minute frequency, every day, helps you get through a lot In a traditional 50-minute therapy session, it's common for people to settle into things, then, right as they're doing some heavy lifting and reaching an insight that's particularly challenging or emotional, the session's over. So, by allowing 90 minutes, you're able to settle in and cover a lot more. Working every day in therapy like this could help him pick right back up where they left off the day before, not only face what's happening that day, what's coming up, and all the pressures, but also get a jumpstart on that intensive work of answering questions like, "Why did this happen? How do I stop this from happening again?" Hopefully, that would be a big part of his motivation for doing this much therapy. This also signals something to his company and to people watching Sometimes coming back into the workplace after such a big public situation requires satisfying people. I think that could also be a part of this. It demonstrates to those watching that someone is working hard on themselves. If multiple affairs are happening, if that is what's happening here, it's easy for people to say, "Look, if you're involved in all of this, how are you paying attention to what's going on at the company?" I would imagine if he came out and said, "Hey, I'm going to do an hour a week of therapy, or I'm going to do two hours a week," that just wouldn't suffice for people. If you're going to make the behavioral change, repair the relationships, and take the helm of the company , yeah, you do have to make changes all over the place to be healthy again. title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade postponed for the first time in its history
summary: Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed due to weather. The annual event is now set for Saturday at 8:30 a.m.
content: Workers deflate balloons on Wednesday night after the parade was postponed to Saturday. Adam Gray/Getty Images Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed to Saturday due to weather. It's the parade's first postponement and the first time it won't march on Thanksgiving since WWII. Over 3.5 million people attend the parade in New York City each year. Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed, disrupting the holiday plans of more than 3.5 million people who typically attend the annual event. The parade is now set for 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, according to a statement from the company, which said the rescheduling was due to weather. A storm forecast to bring strong winds and moderate to heavy rainfall is projected to hit the East Coast during the holiday, according to the National Weather Service in New York. At a press conference on Wednesday evening, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, "I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," standing in front of a star-shaped Macy's balloon. "Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down Sixth Avenue," Mamdani added. "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first." The planned balloon viewing went ahead on Wednesday. Julie Zeveloff Will Coss, vice president and head of Macy's Studios, said at the press conference that the company was "heartbroken" by the postponement, adding that "this parade has been built with love." Macy's said in a statement last year that the parade, which began in New York City in 1924, would make its 100th march in 2026. This is the first time the event has been postponed in its history, and the first time since World War II that the parade will not take place on Thanksgiving , when it was canceled in 1942, 1943, and 1944, as materials that would've been used were diverted to the war effort. The storm has also disrupted a parade in Philadelphia, which calls itself the oldest Thanksgiving parade in the US. Unlike the Macy's parade, the 6abc Dunkin' Thanksgiving Day Parade won't be rescheduled. Instead, it will be a TV-only event that will take place on Thanksgiving morning. Workers deflate a giant Shrek balloon. Adam Gray/Getty Images In New York, images showed workers deflating iconic balloons including Mickey Mouse, Shrek, and Buzz Lightyear on Wednesday night after the postponement was announced. The postponement has left a wave of people, including tourists and parade performers, scrambling to make last-minute accommodations. Pearland High School's 500-member band is among the groups scrambling to change plans. The Texas district said keeping students in New York through Saturday could add nearly $400,000 in unplanned hotel and flight costs, and it launched a donation drive to help cover them. The disruption has also upset visitors who booked a Thanksgiving-only trip to see the milestone 100th parade. On social media, visitors said that they planned to have reunions around the parade, with family flying in from different parts of the country. Some tourists said they are paying premium prices to rebook flights and hotels, while others said their bucket-list trips would remain unfulfilled because they find it unaffordable to extend their stays. Erin Finney, who traveled with her family from Lakeland, Florida, to New York City to catch the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, said that it had been on her bucket list since she was a child. "When I got to the subway, I sat down at the station and started crying. I kept thinking, "Why am I crying?" But I think it was all the excitement leading up to it, and how disappointed I was that I wouldn't get to see the parade after all," she told Business Insider. She added, "I looked into changing our flights, but it would have cost at least another $800, plus extra nights at the hotel and food for all of us." Amanda Goh contributed reporting. title: It's not Thanksgiving déjà vu: NBC is replacing the postponed Macy's parade with a rerun of last year's
summary: Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade is taking a rain check due to severe weather, so last year's edition will be aired on NBC instead on Thursday.
content: A Labubu on Pop Mart's float for last year's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Michael Simon/Getty Images for POP MART Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade is taking a rain check. NBC is going to re-air last year's edition on Thursday instead. Organizers will deflate the balloons, take them back to New Jersey, then re-inflate them for Saturday. As Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade takes a rain check for its landmark 100th edition, NBC is airing a replay instead. The network will show last year's parade on Thursday at 8:30 a.m. ET/CT/MT and 7:30 a.m. PT, after severe weather forced organizers to move the event to Saturday. That means another outing for Cynthia Erivo's opening performance of "Feeling Good," and the singers from "KPop Demon Hunters" performing "Golden." Busta Rhymes, Ciara, Shaggy, and Teyana Taylor also appeared in the 99th edition, hosted by Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker. But some of the floats might already feel a bit dated looking back, like one for "Stranger Things" — which aired its final season last year — plus some Labubus . New York City officials warned of heavy rain, coastal flooding, and gusts reaching 60 to 65 mph on Thursday, with the strongest winds expected in the afternoon and evening. "There is no destination worth risking your safety," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. The rescheduled parade is due to start Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, airing on NBC and streaming on Peacock. "While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," Will Coss , the parade's executive producer, said during a Wednesday news conference with city officials. Moving a show this big takes some juggling. Coss said the balloons would be deflated, returned to a facility in New Jersey, then inflated again for Saturday's parade. The parade first took place in 1924 and was canceled from 1942 to 1944 during World War II. In 1971, bad weather grounded the balloons, but the parade went ahead. title: Making MrBeast: How Jimmy Donaldson went from shy kid to YouTube's top creator and built a business worth billions
summary: MrBeast is the top YouTuber on earth with the most subscribers. But the 28-year-old, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, keeps some details private.
content: Beast Industries is trying to expand beyond its famous founder, Jimmy Donaldson. Sujit JAISWAL / AFP via Getty Images Jimmy "MrBeast" Donaldson went from growing up in a small city to becoming the king of YouTube. The 28-year-old is seeking to build a Disney-style content empire with multiple consumer brands. It hasn't been easy. Donaldson has weathered scandals and lawsuits along the way. MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, is the biggest YouTuber on earth. For an influencer, the 28-year-old keeps some personal details close to the vest. Donaldson's unlikely rise started in Greenville, North Carolina — the small city where he still resides and where his burgeoning company, Beast Industries , is headquartered. Beyond online stardom, Donaldson has taken Hollywood by storm with his hit streaming show, " Beast Games ." He's also building a slew of consumer brands and services in a quest to create a company in the vein of Disney . Donaldson has also made charity work a key part of his career and personal mission through Beast Philanthropy , and has de-emphasized his own personal wealth despite his vast ambitions. Here's everything you need to know about who MrBeast is and how he's built his career. Early life and background MrBeast was born James Stephen Donaldson on May 7, 1998, and grew up in Greenville, North Carolina . After Donaldson's parents separated, his mother, Sue, raised Donaldson and his older brother CJ as a single parent, he said on "The Diary of a CEO" podcast. Donaldson has said he prefers not to speak about his dad. Donaldson was an extremely quiet child growing up and didn't have many friends, he said on the "Dhar & Jay Show." From an early age, Donaldson was obsessed with YouTube and uploaded his first video under the username MrBeast6000. Initially, Donaldson tried to game the YouTube algorithm with different types of videos — from "let's play" gaming streams to commentary videos about other YouTubers. At the time, he was mostly off-camera. Jimmy Donaldson and Thea Booysen, also a content creator, tied the knot in July 2026. Jean Catuffe/Getty Images Unlike some other creators who are an open book, Donaldson keeps mum about many personal details, including his political beliefs. That said, he frequently discusses living with Crohn's disease, an inflammatory bowel disease . On the relationships front, Donaldson proposed to his now-wife, Thea Booysen , the content creator and novelist, on Christmas in 2024. They wed on a private island in July 2026. MrBeast's rise on YouTube After experimenting with different kinds of videos, Donaldson went viral in 2017 for a video in which he counted from zero to 100,000, a feat he said took more than 40 hours. That year, he surpassed 1 million subscribers. Other early stunts included reading every word in the dictionary and spinning a fidget spinner for 24 hours. Endurance and last-person-to-leave challenges are still his bread and butter, even as the productions have grown in budget and scope. In 2020, the average MrBeast video cost $300,000 to make, Bloomberg reported . By 2024, that figure was roughly $3.5 million, he told the creators of "The Colin and Samir Show." Over time, Donaldson started enacting big-budget stunts with an altruistic bent, such as tipping thousands of dollars to lesser-known Twitch streamers, waitresses, and Uber drivers. By 2018, he said he'd given away $1 million. Donaldson's friends and collaborators over the years have included Nolan Hansen, Chandler Hallow, Tareq Salameh, Karl Jacobs, and Mack Hopkins. Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for Prime Video Donaldson is also known for fastidiously fine-tuning his thumbnails and video titles to maximize engagement. Donaldson surpassed the Indian production company T-Series as the most-subscribed-to YouTube channel in June 2024. His main MrBeast channel has more than 500 million subscribers. His most popular long-form video, "$456,000 Squid Game In Real Life!," has more than 987 million views. He's also the third most-followed creator on TikTok, with nearly 148 million followers. MrBeast's business ventures While brand deals helped fuel Donaldson's ambitious early videos, his business has ballooned into a nearly 800-person operation that investors have valued at more than $5 billion. Today, it blends media, advertising, chocolate bars, fintech, and more — with ambitions for an IPO. His company, Beast Industries, generated $473 million in revenue in 2024, according to a pitch deck obtained by Business Insider. The company expected that figure to roughly double in 2025. Still, Donaldson said in February 2025 that he had less than $1 million in his bank account, as he prefers to reinvest profits back into the company. Because of this, Donaldson's net worth is largely comprised of his stake in Beast Industries. Beast Industries' businesses include the candy brand Feastables , the packaged food brand Lunchly , a collectible action-figure line dubbed MrBeast Lab, and Viewstats, an analytics platform for creators. Donaldson is embroiled in a legal battle with Virtual Dining Concepts , his former partner in the ghost-kitchen business MrBeast Burger . He sued the company, alleging it made "terrible quality" burgers under his name, and Virtual Dining Concepts fired back with a breach-of-contract suit. The suits are scheduled to go to trial in December. Donaldson is embroiled in a lawsuit with his former partner in MrBeast Burger. MrBeast Burger On the media front, Donaldson has grown his content operation beyond YouTube. He did a $100 million deal for an Amazon Prime Video show, "Beast Games." While it drove record viewership for Amazon , Donaldson said he lost tens of millions on the first season. Amazon gave it a vote of confidence, renewing it for two more seasons. Donaldson has stepped back from running parts of his company, appointing former Shutterfly chief executive Jeffrey Housenbold as CEO in 2024 and subsequently hiring a slew of seasoned execs. He's also tried to lessen the company's reliance on him. He's developing various content verticals to be hosted by different creators. In September, he published a novel alongside author James Patterson, which debuted at No. 12 on Amazon's new releases chart. About a year ago, he premiered an animated series, "MrBeast Lab: The Descent ." The show was based on a MrBeast toy line that became a best-selling new toy property in 2024, according to Circana's retail sales tracking. New episodes were released this fall. Looking beyond media, Donaldson has discussed plans to expand into new areas, including financial services through the recently acquired Step app, mobile phone plans, and an influencer marketplace . He's also shared plans for a membership program . MrBeast's philanthropy and social impact Over the years, Donaldson has incorporated his knack for virality into various charity efforts, including a 2019 campaign to plant 20 million trees , which Elon Musk contributed to. Donaldson's philanthropic work includes his own charity organization, Beast Philanthropy . However, at times, some of this work has backfired, such as when he was accused of gifting eye surgeries for clout . Donaldson has shrugged off the criticism and said he plans to give away "every penny" he makes to help people before he dies. Despite his success, Donaldson has often discussed how he prefers to eschew the finer things in life. "No matter how big I get I'll never own a mansion, yacht, Lamborghini etc," he tweeted in 2022. "All I want is to make the best videos possible and help as many people as I can while doing it." MrBeast allegations, criticism, controversy, and lawsuits With great visibility comes great scrutiny. Donaldson has been no stranger to controversy over the years. In 2024, he was involved in multiple scandals . In July 2024, Donaldson's childhood friend and coworker Ava Kris Tyson was accused of inappropriately messaging a 13-year-old . Tyson apologized for "bad edgy jokes" on X but said she'd never groomed anyone. She said that she and Donaldson had "mutually decided" to cut ties. Donaldson said on X that he was "disgusted" by the allegations and had hired a third party to investigate. The investigation into various issues at the company ultimately concluded that claims of sexual misconduct between employees and minors were "without basis." The alleged victim also said on X that the grooming claims were false. Donaldson's hit Amazon competition series "Beast Games" was preceded by controversies. MrBeast / X Donaldson's "Beast Games" series was also beset by controversies. Contestants on the show alleged a number of safety concerns, including a lack of access to food and medical care, and injuries during a preliminary shoot. News of the allegations was first reported by The New York Times. A rep for MrBeast previously told BI that the shoot "was unfortunately complicated by the CrowdStrike incident, extreme weather, and other unexpected logistical and communications issues." One former "Beast Games" crew member also told BI he was nearly crushed by a concrete-like structure on set in Toronto. After BI contacted Donaldson's team for comment, the crew member said a production rep had contacted him, saying they were "here to support me and provided me some things I can't share." Five of the contestants on the show filed a class-action lawsuit in September 2024, alleging sexual harassment and dangerous conditions. The case is pending. In November 2024, Donaldson addressed some of the allegations around the show on X, saying they were "blown out of proportion." Around the same time as the "Beast Games" controversy, Donaldson also acknowledged an old clip that resurfaced on social media in which he could be seen making homophobic and racist comments. A spokesperson said in a statement to multiple outlets at the time that Donaldson "repeatedly apologized and has learned that increasing influence comes with increased responsibility." title: The US Navy wants drones to work alongside warships. Sometimes they're better off on their own, defense analysts say.
summary: A new report argues that pairing Navy drones with crewed warships can limit their advantages, including flexibility, adaptability, and affordability.
content: A new report analyzes the US Navy's plans for the future fleet and offers several key takeaways. US Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Andrew Langholf Pairing drones with warships isn't always the best approach, defense analysts say. Drones operating separately from crewed ships could be more flexible and effective. The approach could shape how the US uses drones to counter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. The US Navy wants naval drones to help its crewed warships do more, but a new report argues that making them work together might not always be the best approach. Sometimes, drones might prove more useful on their own, defense analysts wrote. The US military has experimented with crewed-uncrewed teaming for years, focusing on how uncrewed systems can complement crewed naval elements by extending reach, sensing, and firepower. But forced manned-unmanned teaming can limit their biggest advantages, specifically their flexibility and the ability to take risks that humans can't. In a new report from the Hudson Institute think tank, authors Bryan Clark, David Byrd, and Dan Patt analyze the Navy's plan to grow the fleet, proposing a more affordable design and structure that adapts to new threats and embraces emerging technologies. Discussing a new theory of victory for the Navy, the authors argue that pairing crewed and uncrewed platforms "tend to suboptimize both the manned and unmanned components of the team and fail to exploit the advantages of each." For example, uncrewed ships could carry additional munitions for crewed vessels, but limitations in speed, range, and protection could demand more frequent refueling and the use of defensive escorts, potentially defeating the purpose of using a naval drone in the first place. Furthermore, drones that aren't equally low-observable could compromise nearby stealthier platforms, while fixing that could get expensive, sacrificing their affordability. Meanwhile, deploying drones alongside crewed warships could undermine the ability to quickly modify and adapt the uncrewed systems. "Manned platforms cannot change sensors, EW [electronic warfare] systems, C2 [command and control] software, or weapons quickly because engineers need to assess the impact on safety and other systems," the report says. Autonomous systems can be modified much faster but could be subject to the same limitations if operating nearby. Clark, Byrd, and Patt provided several real-world examples that demonstrate how uncrewed technologies can operate as independent units. Over the past year, for instance, Ukrainian troops have expanded their use of uncrewed ground vehicles (UGVs) for logistics and medical evacuations, as well as engineering and fire support. Ukraine has increased its employment of ground robots throughout this year, especially for logistics operations and medical evacuations. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images "These operations deliberately use unmanned systems for operations or in places where the Ukrainian commanders do not want to risk human troops, increasingly producing a human-free front line," the authors write. In less-contested environments, soldiers and ground robots can work together, but communications problems, difficult terrain, and the need to refuel and repair robots can complicate operations, potentially putting accompanying troops at risk. The authors argue that the more hands-off approach to uncrewed systems could help the US military counter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. According to the Hudson report, recent Navy Integrated Battle Problems examining a potential Chinese invasion have experimented with using autonomous systems in ways that draw on lessons from Ukrainian, Iranian, and Houthi operations. "By attacking troop transports and their escorts with drone boats, undersea vehicles, and loitering munitions, a force of mostly RAS [robotics and autonomous systems] could slow or disrupt the invasion. This would give US and allied forces targeting information and time to destroy PLA [People's Liberation Army] ships with long-range missiles and torpedo fires," the authors write. US military officials have also explored using large numbers of drones to disrupt Chinese invasion forces in the Taiwan Strait. Adm. Samuel Paparo, the head of US Pacific Command, has referred to it as an "unmanned hellscape" that would effectively act as a first line of defense and buy US, allied, and partner forces time to respond. Clark, Byrd, and Patt's observations come as the US military figures out the roles of uncrewed systems and autonomy and when it's better to use them together with crewed assets or independently. The Navy has looked at drone boats for port security and also used them for rescue and attack missions in the Middle East. The Hudson report's argument isn't that drones should never work alongside crewed ships, but the Navy could get more out of them by giving them missions that take advantage of what they can do on their own. title: OpenAI's pricing mix-up means most users of its new AI models will hit limits faster
summary: OpenAI said a billing mistake let some users do more within their usage limits than intended with GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol.
content: OpenAI said it resolved a billing error that allowed some users to do more than intended within their usage limits. VCG/VCG via Getty Images OpenAI accidentally gave users a discount on its new models. Users of 6.2 Astra and Sol will now start hitting their usage limits 40% and 25% faster, an OpenAI exec said. Users and AI companies are both grappling with compute costs, especially as agents become more popular. Black Friday savings briefly and unintentionally came to OpenAI. The company made a billing mistake that "incorrectly discounted" GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol earlier this month, Thibault Sottiaux, the engineering lead for Codex, OpenAI's coding agent, said on X. Now that it's been fixed, most users can expect to hit their usage limits 40% and 25% faster on Astra and Sol, respectively, for doing the same tasks, Sottiaux said in his early-morning post on Thursday. Astra is OpenAI's newest frontier model for the most difficult tasks, whereas Sol is cheaper and for everyday tasks, according to OpenAI's website. Sottiaux said OpenAI wouldn't retroactively charge users for the difference in past usage with the new models, which both launched on November 17. "As a small token to apologize for the mistake, we'll be adding one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business," Sottiaux wrote, meaning everyone on the listed paid plans gets one opportunity to reset their usage limit early. Usage limits are measured in tokens , the basic unit of data inputted or outputted by an AI model. More intensive tasks require more compute, and therefore rack up a higher token bill. Different ChatGPT subscriptions have different limits, and pricing plans across models have become a moving target for AI companies. This isn't Sottiaux's first X post about problems with usage limits . In June, some Codex users reported reaching their usage limits more quickly than usual, even when performing the same tasks. OpenAI set up a "warroom" to look into the issue, Sottiaux said at the time, and eventually determined that Codex was doing more behind-the-scenes work than intended, causing it to use more compute. The company also reset everyone's limits in that scenario. Coding tasks can get expensive quickly for users, since they typically use more compute compared to basic tasks like asking a chatbot a question. Companies, too, are grappling with ballooning AI bills , as employees burn through tokens and cash. JPMorgan, for example, instituted $2,000 monthly caps for some of its engineers using Claude Code earlier this year. Yet agents for both coding and mundane tasks are also pricey for AI companies, and questions remain about how they will make money. Earlier this month, Elon Musk said the cost of maintaining SpaceX's GrokBot , an AI agent, was "unsustainably high relative to revenue." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told investors in October that Muse, the wildly popular AI agent, isn't making money yet and is "very compute-intensive." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: An exec who helped turn Starlink into SpaceX's cash machine is leaving
summary: Chad Gibbs, Starlink's VP of business operations, is leaving SpaceX after more than a decade, according to an internal email seen by Business Insider.
content: Starship carries Starlink satellites into orbit on the rocket's November test flight. Ricardo ARDUENGO / AFP via Getty Images A longtime Starlink executive is leaving SpaceX, according to an internal email seen by Business Insider. VP Chad Gibbs oversaw Starlink Mobile and the service's supply chain and operations teams. His departure comes as SpaceX makes moves to turn Starlink into a major mobile carrier. SpaceX has lost a longtime executive overseeing some operations at Starlink , its money-spinning satellite internet division. Chad Gibbs, SpaceX's vice president of business operations, is leaving the company after more than a decade, according to an internal announcement seen by Business Insider. The McKinsey alumnus oversaw the growth of Starlink's Mobile service , as well as the satellite internet network's supply chain, sales, and customer support teams. Gibbs' LinkedIn page has been changed to "SpaceX Alum" and lists a departure date of November 2026. In an email sent to employees on Friday announcing a "significant org change," Starlink chief Michael Nicolls thanked Gibbs for "a decade of massive contributions" to SpaceX and Starlink, and wished him a "well-deserved break." Nicolls did not say whether Gibbs would be taking on another role elsewhere, or who would take over his responsibilities. SpaceX and Gibbs did not respond to requests for comment. Gibbs' departure, which has not previously been reported, comes at a critical time for Starlink. The satellite internet service has grown from a side project to a major moneymaker over the past six years. Last year, Starlink was responsible for more than 60% of SpaceX's revenue . Revenue from SpaceX's connectivity division, which is mostly Starlink, grew to $5.25 billion in Q3 this year. SpaceX is now working to transform Starlink , which uses a constellation of 11,000 satellites in low-Earth orbit to provide internet across the globe, from a boutique service for adventurers and digital nomads into a major mobile carrier and connectivity powerhouse. Elon Musk's rocket launcher has been snapping up spectrum bands in the US in a quest to take on AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon. SpaceX recently announced a deal with Qualcomm to collaborate on a network of tens of thousands of cellular ground stations, with construction expected to begin next year. SpaceX is also seeking regulatory approval to launch as many as 100,000 new Starlink satellites in the coming years. However, the expanded Starlink constellation would be dwarfed by Starmind , a network of 1 million orbital data centers that received the green light from US regulators on Wednesday. Gibbs' departure is the latest change to SpaceX's org chart in recent months. Business Insider previously reported that SpaceX had reshuffled the leadership of its growing compute business in October, placing former Starship executive Kevin Holland in charge of the company's giant Memphis data centers. title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving with flight delays, cancellations, and power outages across the US
summary: Coastal flooding, strong winds, and heavy rainfall are expected to batter the East Coast this Thanksgiving.
content: A storm is hitting the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel with flight delays and cancellations across the US. Around 600,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled. Bad weather has even led to the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Parade. Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel, with more severe weather expected to hit the East Coast on Thursday. More than 6,500 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed on Wednesday, and about 160 were canceled, according to FlightAware. As of about 11:30 a.m. ET Thursday, roughly 1,000 flights had been delayed and 400 canceled. The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving. Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. Over 600,000 US households were without power on Thursday morning, according to PowerOutage.us. That included about 200,000 in Virginia and 150,000 in Missouri. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast. One in four flights departing Baltimore/Washington International were canceled, but no other major airport had a cancellation rate above 10%, according to FlightAware. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour. On Thursday morning, LaGuardia Airport recorded wind gusts of up to 39 knots, or 45 miles per hour. While such strong winds can disrupt flying, most flights at New York's airports were operating normally as of Thursday morning. Mamdani said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled. "The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel. The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights. The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. Disruption was worsened in Miami when a FedEx plane overshot the runway on Wednesday evening. No injuries were reported, but the incident caused inbound flights to be grounded for about 90 minutes. title: Thomson Reuters is using both American and Chinese AI for its next model
summary: Thomson Reuters blends Google's Gemma and Z.ai's GLM to build Thomson 1.1, hoping to cut AI costs by using both Chinese and US open-source models.
content: Thomson Reuters CEO Steve Hasker. John Lamparski/Getty Images for Advertising Week New York Forget the AI race: Thomson Reuters wants the best of both worlds. The company's next AI model is built off Google's Gemma and Z.ai's GLM, it tells Business Insider. The data and legal giant has spent $40 million so far building its own chatbots. As China and the US race to compete on AI, Thomson Reuters, the Canadian data and legal giant, is having it both ways. The company is launching a new AI model called Thomson 1.1 by the end of the year, it tells Business Insider exclusively — and it's built on open-source models from both countries: China's GLM, from Z.ai, and Google's Gemma. By using open-source models that anyone can download and host, Thomson Reuters hopes to reduce its AI costs and take more control over its intellectual property. There's a battle in tech over which AI corporations will use. It pits cheaper Chinese open-source models against closed ones from giants like Anthropic and OpenAI. US companies like Google, Meta, and Thinking Machines Lab have also released powerful open-source models in recent months. It's a shift for Thomson Reuters , which didn't use American AI for its previous in-house model, Thomson 1.0. Instead, it built its chatbot off Qwen, an AI from the Chinese tech giant Alibaba. "The US government, and many other governments around the world, prefer to have US and Western sovereign models at the foundation of what we do," Thomson Reuters' chief technology officer, Joel Hron, told Business Insider. "Where we can, we're going to use Western and US-based labs to ground Thomson." Hron said the company still uses Z.ai's GLM because it excels at using computers — a key feature of AI agents . It also chose Google's Gemma because of its small size and efficiency, he added. Thomson Reuters aims to build an AI that helps its clients with mid-tier work, such as tax advice. For the most difficult tasks, it still plans to use OpenAI and Anthropic. "There's a lot of work that happens in the middle, and that's where we get real economic benefit," Hron said. Open source has its limitations It takes a lot of money for a big company to build a custom AI chatbot, even if it uses free, open-source models. Hron told Business Insider that so far, Thomson Reuters has spent about $40 million on the effort to tweak and tune its own models. That money goes to things like chips, data, and salaries for AI researchers. Adoption is early. Less than 5% of all AI tokens used at Thomson Reuters come from its own AI, Hron said — although that is set to ramp up in the coming years as its focus areas expand. Chinese models also have built-in censorship features that can be tricky to unwind. Hirundo, a startup in Israel, sent Business Insider an analysis showing that one version of the current Thomson model parrots Chinese government talking points. For example, it refused to acknowledge the Tiananmen Square massacre and said that "Taiwan is an inalienable part of China." A Thomson Reuters spokesperson said that its AI handles such questions "substantially better" when it's used as intended — with a set of instructions to follow. The company's coming AI model further reduces bias, the spokesperson added. To large companies hit by high token bills — like Pinterest , AT&T, and others — the appeal of open source remains strong: it can reduce recurring AI costs and give companies technology they own and control. "Thomson is what AI sovereignty actually looks like in practice," Andrew Bean, Thomson Reuters' lead AI scientist, said. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I spent 2 nights in a tiny home hotel in Germany. 8 things surprised me about the 2-story, 100-square-foot house.
summary: From its tubular two-story shape to its smart tech and clever storage hacks, I was blown away by the tiny home I booked in Germany.
content: The reporter stayed in a 100-square-foot accommodation at a tiny home hotel in Germany. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My Airbnb for two nights in Germany was unlike any tiny home I'd stayed in before. It looked more like a giant can of soda. The 100-square-foot cylinder had three rooms, two floors, and zero corners. There's something extra satisfying about occupying a space that is so efficiently used. Seeing clever storage hacks and multipurpose furniture that make a tiny home feel larger is like visual ASMR to me. That's why I choose to stay in little accommodations around the world. I've spent a night in a lifeguard tower in Miami, an Airstream trailer in Austria, and a barrel abode in Switzerland . I've slept in overnight train cabins in the US and Europe and 400-square-foot containers on wheels. But I don't think any of those past stays were as impressive as the tiny home hotel in Germany that I booked for two nights in 2022. The $70-a-night accommodation surprised me with its design, technology, and space-saving solutions. While surfing Airbnb for budget stays near Berlin, I was shocked to find a home in Neustrelitz that was tinier than any I've seen in the US at 100 square feet. Slube, a tiny home hotel in Neustrelitz, Germany. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The accommodation was part of a tiny-home hotel called Slube, which designs minimalist concrete "Slubes" for up to two adults and one child, according to the company's website . Slube has three locations around Germany. The location in Neustrelitz has 10 accommodations. There are three types of Slubes: Basic, which is one story; Home, which is two stories; and Tower, which adds a rooftop terrace. I booked a Slube Home for two nights for $140. It was 16 feet tall with two floors totaling 106 square feet. It had a lounging area, a bathroom, and a loft bedroom. It was less than half the size of any tiny home I'd booked in the US. The concept of a tiny cylindrical home was completely new to me. The interior and exterior of the author's accommodation. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I'd never stayed in a tiny home remotely resembling this tubular shape before. Even the livable barrel I booked in Switzerland wasn't quite as unique, given its one-story layout inside. I was surprised by the home's shape and excited by the prospect of sleeping in a tiny space fashioned like a standing cylinder. Upon arrival, I was surprised that the home had high-tech features I'd never seen before. I checked in with my phone and controlled the room temperature from bed. Smart controls on the author's phone. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When I arrived at the tiny home by train from the airport in Berlin, there didn't seem to be any employees on the property. An email from Slube informed me I'd be staying in room five and could check in by myself using a code sent to my phone. In the past, a host has always either met me or provided directions to the key location on the property. So it was a pleasant surprise that I didn't have to keep track of a key during my stay for the first time. Once inside, I found that the Slube had additional smart features I hadn't seen before. I controlled the lights and temperature on each floor of the home from my phone, which I accessed via my web browser. This made my stay feel a little more luxurious than expected, since I never had to get out of bed to adjust either control. It was my first time staying in a tiny home with a ladder. A view from the top of the ladder. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Each story was 53 square feet. The first level included the bathroom, a sitting area with a foldout table and coffee nook, and a ladder to the second lofted floor, where I'd be sleeping. This was my first time climbing a ladder in a tiny home to reach my bed (save for upper train bunks ). I thought climbing was easy, but it could be challenging for some. There was a latched gate at the top of the ladder, which I imagine was built to keep people safe from falling. This made me feel like a kid in a playhouse, which was fun. Upstairs, I wasn't expecting to have a nightstand in a 53-square-foot bedroom. Joey Hadden/Business Insider After staying in tiny spaces so often, I no longer expect to have a bedside table to store my electronics and water bottle. And this bedroom was smaller than most. So I was surprised when I spotted a lower platform surrounding the bed that doubled as a nightstand. It had easily accessible outlets, a pocket for the TV remote, and more space for my belongings, including my water bottle. This saved me from having to go down the ladder every time I was thirsty, which I appreciated. Back downstairs, the bathroom didn't feel as cramped as I thought it would. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The bathroom took up about half of the first floor, making it about 26 square feet. I was initially concerned that I might feel as cramped as I did in Amtrak's sleeper-train bedroom, where the showerhead was above the toilet. To my surprise, the bathroom felt spacious. It was designed unlike any I'd seen, with a shower curtain separating the showerhead and sink from the toilet and storage space. I thought the shower was positioned far enough away from the toilet to make them feel like two separate rooms. On the first floor, I was surprised I didn't have to sacrifice privacy to let natural light in through the windows. Windows in the tiny home. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When I stay in tiny homes, I always appreciate letting in as much natural light as possible because it makes the space feel bigger. But I often stay close to busy streets or other homes and prefer to shut the window curtains for privacy, leaving me in a tight, dark space. Since this was a hotel with other tiny homes nearby, I expected a similar situation. But all the windows on the first floor had a film covering most of the glass, so I could keep the curtains open without worrying that other guests could see inside. I had never seen this in a tiny home before, and I loved not having to sacrifice natural light for privacy. I thought it was a great tool that could be applied to any home in proximity to other people. Somehow, the tiniest home I'd ever experienced was also among the most comfortable, and that was the most surprising part. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I thought these surprising attributes made this tiny home feel more comfortable than most while leaving no space unused. I highly recommend it to tiny-space enthusiasts like me around the world. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Ukraine's fight showed the British Army it needs to be digging trenches in different shapes and places
summary: Ukraine showed the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst that trenches need turns to protect from grenades and are much more vulnerable in open fields.
content: Watching Ukraine, the British Army has changed how it trains its future leaders for trench warfare. John Moore/Getty Images The British Army is changing how it trains future leaders for trench warfare based on lessons from Ukraine. Cadets are digging L-shaped trenches to better protect themselves from grenades and gunfire. Instead of digging in open fields, cadets now seek tree cover to avoid detection by drones. The war in Ukraine showed the British Army that it was training its future leaders to dig trenches in the wrong shape and in the wrong locations. Defensive trench training for future British Army officers at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst had remained largely unchanged for decades, but the war in Ukraine is changing how cadets are taught to build and defend their positions. Trenches that were once straight now have bends to offer better protection from grenades and gunfire. And instead of digging in open fields, cadets are seeking cover from the drones that have made exposed positions increasingly dangerous. Business Insider recently observed elements of a six-day defensive exercise for officer cadets on England's Salisbury Plain. Lessons from Ukraine's battlefields are being incorporated into the training. A Ukrainian officer is also on site to share his experiences and answer questions on modern warfare. The goal of the training is to be "as realistic as possible" about the realities of modern warfare, Brigadier Nick Wight-Boycott, the commander of the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, told Business Insider. Achieving that has meant reconsidering long-standing practices based on lessons from Ukraine. Wight-Boycott said it's about preparing for the kind of "operations the British Army might be asked to do." A different trench shape The resurgence of trench warfare in Ukraine has driven partner militaries to give it more attention in training. At Sandhurst, that means making trenches L-shaped, Wight-Boycott said. Previously, "they were just straight," he said. "If you dropped a grenade in, all the shrapnel just went one way, and everybody who was in the trench would probably get a bit of the fragmentation." British officer cadets are digging small, L-shaped trenches that would be connected if they had more time. Sinéad Baker With L-shaped trenches, "if someone does throw a grenade in, you can hide around the other side, and you're not going to get any of the frag," he said. "Or if someone gets in and they start shooting, you could hide behind it." Capt. Will Kriehn, a British platoon commander, told Business Insider that previously trenches in the exercise were "essentially a deep hole." Now, they're focusing on the new shape because it's what they're seeing in Ukraine. Business Insider observed small groups of officer cadets digging independent L-shaped trenches close together. In a real conflict, the goal would be to dig further to link the trenches. "If we had more time, we would connect them," Kriehn said. Zero, an advising Ukrainian officer who has served as a platoon commander on Ukraine's front lines, told Business Insider that the change is a positive development. Ukrainian troops and unit representatives have said trenches with turns better protect troops from the kind of threats becoming more pervasive in battle. Ideally, they've said in local media interviews, trenches should not have long, straight sections. Elements of the US Army have made similar observations on survivability from the war in Ukraine. Citing observations of conflict, a 2024 US Army Center for Army Lessons Learned report said that "fighting positions should be made as deep as possible with a blocked 'L-shaped' entrance." L-shaped and zigzag trenches are nothing new, having been used in World War I, but Ukraine's war has renewed attention to how these defenses are built and adapted to modern threats. Ukraine's experience has pushed allies to focus more on drone warfare again in their own training. TETIANA DZHAFAROVA/AFP via Getty Images Working with Ukrainians has challenged some British Army assumptions about what trenches actually look like in a modern war. Instead of being clean and surgical, they are likely to be messy, uneven, and full of traps . It's also triggered changes in how the army defends its fighting positions. Wight-Boycott said his officer cadets are using nets and chicken wire to protect fighting positions from grenades and drones, drawing those lessons from Ukraine. Digging away from the open The hills of the Salisbury Plain were scarred by old trenches dug in open fields. Kriehn said that when he did the exercise in 2022, cadets were "deployed into an open field" where they dug for days and "there was no cover." Now, cadets are digging under trees, reflecting lessons from Ukraine about how easily reconnaissance drones can spot exposed positions. Officer cadets used to dig in open fields, but now work under tree cover. Sinéad Baker "In the past," Wight-Boycott said, "they've basically gone into an empty field in the middle of Salisbury Plain and dug trenches where you can see the whole of the field." But, he continued, "everything that we've seen in warfare, not just in Ukraine, is that nobody ever digs in an open field." The training also wants officer cadets to be faster at digging and moving between defensive positions. For instance, instead of spending much of an exercise digging and defending a single position, cadets might now practice quickly digging in, defending, and falling back to do it all over again. The intent is to slow an enemy advance and buy time for other forces to counterattack. The new approach at Sandhurst doesn't mean a change for everything the British Army does. Officers leaving Sandhurst may be deployed away from Europe, or face a conflict that needs different defenses. But the army is preparing for a potential land war with Russia in Europe, and wants its future leaders to be ready to adapt to different threats and battlefield conditions. Sandhurst wants "to make them agile leaders, thinking leaders so that when they leave, no matter what job they go into, they can apply those skill sets to them," Kriehn said. For Sandhurst, new knowledge comes in part from its instructors training Ukrainian soldiers , who have "seen how the Ukrainians have changed their tactics," Wight-Boycott said, and brought that knowledge back. "We've adapted really quickly to that changing character of conflict." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: The US Army tested whether it could still deploy forces to war if attacks knocked out comms at American ports
summary: The Army rehearsed restoring communications at US deployment hubs after simulated attacks knocked networks offline.
content: Army vehicles are loaded onto the USNS Charlton at Joint Base Charleston, South Carolina, March 25, 2024. Tech. Sgt. Alex Fox Echols III/US Air Force The Army simulated attacks that knocked regular communications offline at US deployment hubs. Troops used backup networks to reconnect units and restore access to cargo-tracking systems. More than 85% of US combat power is based in the continental US, a top general previously told lawmakers. The US Army tested whether it could keep communicating with units at American ports after simulated attacks knocked their normal networks offline, rehearsing how it would deploy forces overseas if critical infrastructure at home came under attack. During a recent homeland defense exercise at Fort Eustis, Virginia, the Army's 597th Transportation Brigade used backup communications to connect with units in South Carolina and Texas. The drill simulated physical and cyberattacks that knocked military and commercial networks offline, creating a "catastrophic communications blackout" at key deployment hubs, according to an Army news release. Troops had to restore access to a key system that tracks military cargo moving by air and sea. Losing those connections could make it tougher to track equipment, ensure it reaches the right ports and ships, and move forces overseas on schedule. The service said in the release that the exercise proved successful, though it did not provide deeper details on the amount of stress put on the system, or any persistent challenges More than 85% of US combat power resides in the continental United States, Gen. Randall Reed, the head of US Transportation Command, told lawmakers in March, making the military's ability to swiftly move troops and equipment vital for a major conflict or national emergency. "A disconnected mobility force threatens the Joint Force's ability to win," Reed wrote in his testimony, calling for communications that can resist jamming and cyberattacks. The threat isn't limited solely to military networks. Potential adversaries could also target civilian infrastructure that US forces depend on. Some US military experts have characterized the current threat situation as "the end of strategic sanctuary ." In February 2024, US cybersecurity and intelligence agencies warned that China-backed Volt Typhoon hackers had compromised critical infrastructure , including transportation and communications networks, positioning themselves to cause disruption during a major crisis or conflict. More recently, refrigeration systems in military commissaries have seen power outages linked to suspected malicious attacks. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I revisited my old college town years after I graduated. It really changed how I think about going back.
summary: Returning to visit my college town after graduating surprised me. My favorite spots were gone, and I felt odd being a tourist instead of a student,
content: I stayed at a new hotel in the college town where I went to school. My favorite spots were gone, and I didn't feel how I expected Courtesy of Lexi Marshall My sister and I stayed at a new hotel in the college town where we had gone to school years earlier. A lot of our favorite spots were gone, and it was hard to feel like an outsider in a familiar place. Making new memories and giving myself permission to just be a visitor helped the trip feel less sad. The mountains looked exactly the way I remembered them. That was the first thing I noticed as my sister and I drove into Boulder, Colorado , on a weekday afternoon. It was comforting, at least until we reached the neighborhood where we had spent so much of our college years. We both attended the University of Colorado Boulder, a few years apart, and now live in Denver . Although the town is only a short drive away, neither of us had stayed near campus since graduating. When a new boutique hotel opened a few blocks from where we used to live, booking a night felt like an obvious excuse for a getaway. I pictured a weekend of making late-night pizza runs, drinking at familiar bars, and wandering streets we once knew by heart. The irony wasn't lost on me: The hotel sits where some of the neighborhood's longtime businesses once operated. It was part of the very transformation that had made our old haunts disappear. I knew things had changed before arriving, but I wasn't prepared for how strange it would feel to see it firsthand. Returning to our old college neighborhood felt like stepping into someone else's memories A look back at my college years, when the neighborhood was filled with familiar businesses and hangouts that have since closed. Courtesy of Lexi Marshall After dropping our bags off at the hotel, we set out with a mental list of places from our college days we wanted revisit. The first was gone. So was the second. My sister started laughing in the way you do when the alternative is feeling something heavier. We kept walking anyway, checking our memories against the streets like two people holding an outdated map. Some familiar storefronts had been replaced entirely. Others had become something different. Even the neighborhood's familiar noise and energy seemed to have shifted. As students, we never thought of our college town as something that could change so dramatically. It was simply the backdrop to our lives: where we grabbed late-night food, met friends, and walked to class. We assumed certain places would always be there, much like the mountains surrounding the town. That first evening, I realized I wasn't just missing the restaurants and bars. I was missing the version of myself who had a reason to be there. Back then, I belonged automatically. I had a schedule, a place to live, and familiar routes I could navigate half asleep. Now I had a hotel room and a checkout time. There is a particular kind of disorientation in being a stranger somewhere you once knew by heart. I caught myself giving my sister directions to places that no longer existed. I even felt protective of a neighborhood that had never asked me to defend it. We stopped chasing the past and started enjoying the town as visitors The next morning, we tried a different approach. Instead of hunting for what was gone, we picked a direction and set off with no plan. We found a coffee shop in a building I'd walked past countless times without noticing. We explored streets we'd rarely ventured down as students and took recommendations from people at places we'd never visited. Something shifted once we stopped measuring everything against our memories. Without a checklist of old favorites, we started noticing what was actually there. We talked about the neighborhood the way you talk about a friend who has changed, with some nostalgia but also curiosity. By the second night, we had stopped trying to recreate our college years and settled into our hotel's lively bar instead. We ordered drinks we couldn't have afforded as students and stayed awake long past the time we used to have to be up for class. In a way, the hotel became part of the experience we hadn't known we were looking for: a new place to make memories in a town filled with old ones. I realized the town hadn't erased us. It had simply moved on, much as we had. Somewhere between graduation and now, we'd become people who could walk into an unfamiliar place and make it feel like ours. If you're revisiting your college town, leave room for new memories Now, we make different memories than we did back then. Courtesy of Lexi Marshall My biggest takeaway was that returning to a meaningful place doesn't have to mean recreating the experiences you had there. In fact, trying to do so can get in the way of enjoying what's there now. If you're planning a trip back to your college town, leave the checklist at home. Pick one or two traditions worth revisiting, whether that's walking through campus or ordering your old coffee-shop favorite , but leave the rest of the itinerary open. Stay somewhere new, ask locals for recommendations, and give yourself permission to be a visitor. Every version of a college town belongs to someone. The places that closed had their time, and the businesses replacing them are creating memories for a new generation of students . One day, they'll return to find their own favorite spots missing. Maybe that's the real marker of growing up: not that your old map still works, but that you no longer need it to. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Walmart won't resort to 'gimmicks' to get Black Friday shoppers in early
summary: Walmart US chief merchant told Business Insider the retailer is looking to win Black Friday shoppers with great items and deals, not door prizes.
content: Walmart has been running deals since October, but it says it is saving some key discounts for Black Friday. Brian Kaiser/Bloomberg via Getty Images Door prizes have become a popular way for stores to boost Black Friday traffic — but not at Walmart. The company's US chief merchant told BI she intends to win shoppers by offering the best deals. "We're not going to pay people to get in line," she said. Walmart is taking an old-school approach to retail's busiest weekend of the year . Although several retailers are rolling out door prizes like swag bags and gift cards to boost Black Friday visits, Walmart's US chief merchant Julie Barber told Business Insider she's letting the deals do the talking. "We're not going to do gimmicks. We're not going to pay people to get in line. We're going to have amazing items in the store, and that's going to drive people in," she said. That's a sharp contrast with rival Target, which will give away gift cards worth at least $25 to the first hundred shoppers at each of its stores on Black Friday. One winner at each location will get a $1,000 card. Kohl's is likewise offering $5 to $100 gift cards to the first 200 shoppers at its stores, and Lowe's is again giving its Black Friday Buckets to the first 50 rewards members who show up at participating locations. In addition to free Lowe's merchandise, some winners will receive appliances worth up to $2,000. Barber spent this week jetting around the country to check on how Walmart stores — and their competitors — are prepping for the holiday rush. This year, she says Walmart customers are laser-focused on value , with seven in ten survey respondents telling the company that lower prices would make their holiday shopping easier. That translates to the company emphasizing new products and low prices. She said that Thanksgiving week is typically the largest-selling period of the year for TVs, but Walmart is extending Black Friday deals beyond traditional gifts and electronics to offer discounts on more everyday essentials. For example, Walmart will be running a big sale on vehicle tires. Last week, CFO John David Rainey said the online sales growth of more than 20% year over year is more than offsetting a slight decline of in-person shopping. "Between in-store shopping and digital fulfillment, we have more volume going through our US stores than ever before," he said during Walmart's third quarter earnings call. Barber said that her store teams are heading into the holiday rush with the highest inventory levels that they've had all year. "We're set up pretty well, I think, for both the in-store and online shopper," she said. And even though the holiday season is starting earlier and includes more individual sale events on the calendar leading up to Christmas, Barber said her team makes sure there's enough compelling deals to make the annual Black Friday spree worthwhile. "We plan it out where there's something new and special that happens every time we have an event," she said. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: What to do if your Thanksgiving flight is delayed or canceled due to weather
summary: Heavy rainfall is expected across the US during one of the busiest travel weeks. Here's what to do if you get caught up in holiday travel chaos.
content: Here's what to do if you get caught up in holiday travel chaos. Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Storms are expected to bring heavy rainfall across the US on Thanksgiving. Weather is considered an uncontrollable disruption, so airlines aren't required to provide freebies. Here's what you can do if your flight is delayed or canceled. Holiday travelers have begun to experience some flight delays and cancellations on Thanksgiving as a series of storms hit the US . If you're wondering what your options are if the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out. According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, weather or an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions. That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. It was the same situation during the five-hour nationwide ground stop on November 13 that led to over 12,000 flight cancellations. Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard , which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due weather or other non-controllable factor would not fall under crew scheduling. Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card. Here's what to do if your flight is disrupted. 1. Know your rights as an airline passenger in the US Airline passengers have some customer rights in the US. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events. The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats. If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control. The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations. 2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking options Most airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog. Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person. If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night. Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent. Here are the phone numbers for each airline: Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008 Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888 American: 1-800-433-7300 Avelo: 1-346-616-9500 Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger. Delta: 1-800-221-1212 Frontier: 1-602-333-5925 JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583 Southwest: 1-800-435-9792 United: 1-800-864-8331 3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucher The Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers . Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard. Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher. For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask. It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier. 4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insurance American Express and Chase have travel credit cards. Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance , such as Chase's Sapphire Reserve and American Express' Platinum Card . Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit. For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US. However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs. Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim. 5. Know when to walk away Consider renting a car or taking the train. Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance). If you are stuck in another city and have no other option but to stay in a hotel or wait at the airport, decide how you want to spend your time and make a plan.
